epochs.name: General Availability
epochs.goal: Ship a credible v1-grade language: diagnostics, jet bind, wave-2 packages.

epochs.name: Product Pillars
epochs.goal: Every major language, runtime, library and tooling feature that makes Jet a daily-driver TypeScript/Swift replacement: JIT dev loop + Go-scale async, structured concurrency + coroutines, user derives + typed reflection, full HTTP client/server, stdlib breadth, language ergonomics, IDE-grade semantic tooling, and the reactive UI stack. Excludes the package/OS layer (E4), Jai metaprogramming (E5), and CI/docs (E6).
exitCriteria: Each pillar ships a flagship vertical slice (CLI, server, web, game, freestanding) proving real workflows: docs, tests, packaging, diagnostics, performance, deployment (c123)

epochs.name: jetpack & jetos
epochs.goal: The package-manager and OS layer (jetos is built on jetpack, so the whole ecosystem track lives here): jetpack environments replacing nix-shell, package build-from-source, registry + publish, content-addressed store, monorepo workspaces, package signing, programmable builds, then jetos — a declarative machine with an installable ISO.

epochs.name: Metaprogramming
epochs.goal: Programmable builds and compile-time metaprogramming on E3's reflection/derive foundation: build-as-Jet (fn build(b: BuildContext), D-BUILDENTRY1/D-BUILDPOLICY1), gated build-time I/O, stdlib-only DSL syntax islands (D-EXT1), and reserved derive/bound attributes. Full Jai message loop and proc macros stay parked in E7 (post-self-host, c154); reader macros / grammar mutation closed won't-do (D-EXT1).
exitCriteria: Build-as-Jet programmable build system (BuildContext authority tiers)
Reserved attributes shipped when real cases land (serde bound override)

epochs.name: CI & Documentation
epochs.goal: Release hygiene, CI pipelines, and full adoption + reference documentation — done once the language and libraries are firmly set, so docs and pipelines harden against a stable surface rather than a moving one.

epochs.name: Advanced
epochs.goal: Expert-tier language and runtime controls: explicit opt-in low-level power, sharper performance tuning, and the advanced features that stay out of the beginner path.

epochs.name: Bootstrapping
epochs.goal: Self-hosting and compiler bootstrapping: use Jet to build Jet, tighten the toolchain loop, and remove host-side friction from development and release.

cards.title: Memory/allocation controls push: arenas, ref fields, uninit, buffers, opt-in GC
cards.body: Canonical Epoch 3 memory/allocation push. Merges explicit allocation boundaries (#119), visible uninit (#83), opt-in GC (#69), and labeled ref fields (#147) into the arena/allocation inference track. This card owns expert-tier memory controls while preserving safe beginner defaults.
cards.plan:
Canonical memory/allocation implementation plan. Preserve I1: beginner Jet stays safe; expert controls require explicit syntax/imports/audit where applicable.

Build order:
1. Labeled stored references: implement #Ref(Label) field syntax and owner relationship checks; remove stale core.mem gate per owner outcome; migrate old ref[label] diagnostics.
2. Arena allocator inference: keep current arena plan as base; prove region views cannot escape, reset/free invalidates views, and diagnostics remain Jet-owned.
3. Explicit allocation boundaries: audit Core APIs that allocate across caller-owned boundaries; add buffer/allocator-taking variants using existing allocator model; add lint for hidden boundary allocation in expert/perf contexts.
4. Visible uninit: #Uninit binding, explicit type/no initializer parser rules, definite-assignment proof, plain-data restriction, MaybeUninit codegen only after sema proof; E0421-E0424 snapshots.
5. Opt-in GC library: Gc<T> traced handle as library type for cyclic long-running data, explicit import, no default allocation path change, no sema/codegen primitive unless needed for root tracing.

Acceptance: ui snapshots for dangling/escaping refs, uninit misuse, arena use-after-reset, hidden allocation lint; examples for arena parsing, #Ref owner labels, caller buffers, #Uninit fixed buffers, cyclic Gc graph; golden tests; no generated unsafe outside #Unsafe/std-mem internals.

cards.title: Debugger step 2: native DAP/lldb backend (full-feature stepping + editor wiring)
cards.body: D-DBG3 step 2 (the in-session command surface shipped in c52 over the interpreter). Remaining: a native backend that steps the FULL feature set the interpreter declines (E2203: FFI, tasks, #Unsafe, native std), the D-DBG2 --raw-frames expert view, and editor DAP wiring (VS Code/Zed). The ratified command vocabulary (step/next/continue/finish/break/print/locals/backtrace) is fixed and reused; only the native backend + protocol transport remain.
cards.plan: dap-debugger

log.text: [handoff] lldb added to flake.nix devShells.default.packages (was an ad-hoc nixpkgs fetch for verification only). `nix develop -c which lldb` resolves; tests/debug_native.rs's live-gated case reruns clean (5/5 ok, 1.90s) with no manual PATH workaround. The Open Owner-Q ask below is now resolved — owner said add it.

[done] Native lldb backend shipped end-to-end and verified against a REAL live lldb (fetched via nixpkgs for this session; not yet in flake.nix devShell — see Open Owner-Q). Codegen: TStmt::LineMarker + emit_bundle_dbg/compile_for_debug emit `// jet:line N` markers gated by cx.debug_linemap (off by default — zero effect on normal builds, golden tests, or the JIT tier; confirmed via full test suite + `cargo test --workspace` diffing). New Source/Debug/{LineMap,Inferior,Native,Dap}.rs. `jet debug` auto-dispatches interpreter vs native via the SAME E2203 boundary scan (needs_native) — one command, one meaning (I8); `--dap` forces native for editor launch; `--raw-frames` (D-DBG2) shows raw Rust file:line. Reuses the exact ratified (jet) vocabulary (D-DBG3) over both backends. Live-lldb verification surfaced and fixed THREE real bugs a docs-only implementation would have shipped broken: (1) lldb never re-prints a bare prompt over a pipe (echoes command instead) — naive prompt-wait hangs forever, fixed with a sentinel-command read loop; (2) a resume command's own stop banner is asynchronous and can lose a race to the NEXT command's reply — fixed by always deriving position from a synchronous follow-up `bt`, never the resume's own text; (3) the debuggee inherits lldb's stdout by default, so a Jet `print()` can tear a control-channel sentinel in half — fixed by redirecting debuggee stdout/stderr to temp files via `settings set target.output/error-path` and draining them into the transcript. Also loads rustc's own Rust pretty-printer (lldb_lookup.py + lldb_commands, same two files rust-lldb loads) so String/&str locals render as `"text"` instead of raw allocator internals. Tests: 12 new unit tests (LineMap/Inferior, no lldb needed) + tests/debug_native.rs (5 tests, gated on lldb presence like tests/observe.rs gates on rustc — skips clean without it). New example examples/features/189_debug_native.jet (native-only via `use core.fs`) + golden .out. Full regression pass: cargo build/test workspace-relevant targets (debug, debug_native, golden, observe, cli, tir, decisions, dev/JIT) all green. NOT done: DAP JSON-over-stdio server (Dap.rs) is implemented to the documented wire spec but UNTESTED against a real editor (no VS Code/Zed available here) — verify before wiring into editors/zed or vscode launch configs. gdb/Windows explicitly out of scope (phase 1 = lldb/Linux, per the plan).
Pulled back into e3 per owner: IDE tooling is an E3 exit criterion and this closes it (native DAP/lldb backend + editor wiring). e7 tag on 2026-06-30 was a batch sweep, not a deliberate re-exclude.

cards.title: Full HTTP core library — client + server (D-NETDEP1=A, owner-expanded mandate)
cards.body: Owner mandate (2026-06-26, expanding D-NETDEP1=A): Jet ships a full, complete HTTP library — both client AND server — as a core library, better than Go's net/http. D-NETDEP1's approved pure-Rust crate (ureq/minreq) is only the BOOTSTRAP backing c157's build-time fetch(url, sha256:); the native-ize end-state (Epoch-3 dep rule) is a first-party Jet/Rust HTTP stdlib. SCOPE: client (request/response, methods, headers, body, streaming, TLS, redirects, timeouts) + server (listener, router, handler, middleware, request/response types, graceful shutdown). The client+server API surface (naming + shapes) is SYNTAX/stdlib-surface design needing its own decision docs + ballots BEFORE code — drive from a real-world example per owner-anti-repetition + owner-decision-doc-style. NOT this card: c157's fetch backend (ships first against the bootstrap crate).
cards.plan:
Full HTTP core library — client + server (D-NETDEP1=A mandate; D-HTTPLIB1=A function-first mux; D-HTTPLIB2=B split client/server; D-HTTPLIB3=C HTTP/1.1+HTTP/2+WebSocket; D-HTTPLIB4=B rustls TLS — all ratified & in canon). Bootstrap crates (ureq/hyper, tungstenite, rustls/webpki-roots) wired via the stdlib FFI-bridge pattern (emit bridge template text; never add to the jet compiler Cargo.toml; I6 holds — never in Source/). Native-ize end-state: first-party Jet/Rust HTTP stack.
Staged build: (1) core.http.client — Request/Response, methods, headers, body, streaming, redirects, timeouts, rustls TLS; this also provides the backend for c157's comptime `fetch(url, sha256:)` (record {url,sha256} in .jet/lock) — ship first to unblock c157. (2) core.http.server — listener, function-first `mux` (mux.get/post(path, fn(req:Request)->Response)), `req.params["id"]`, middleware, graceful shutdown. (3) HTTP/2 + WebSocket upgrade. Each stage: examples + goldens; no I4 diagnostics unless misuse surfaces. Big multi-PR track — sequence client before server.

cards.title: Static guarantees push: refinements, contracts, IFC, budgets, bounds, replay soundness
cards.body: Canonical Epoch 3 sema-proof/policy push. Merges information-flow (#24), budgets (#26), formal verification/contracts (#27), out-of-bounds proof escape (#106), and replay soundness (#23) into refinement types (#25). These features share one facts engine/call graph/policy infrastructure and must not grow separate proof systems.
cards.plan:
Canonical static-guarantees implementation plan. Build one sema facts/policy engine, then layer features on it. No duplicate proof engines.

Build order:
1. Facts core: represent refinements as named predicate-backed types; collect comparison/range/require facts; branch narrowing; loop facts; fixed-list length facts; call pre/postcondition facts.
2. Contracts: require/ensure syntax and runtime/test checks where ratified; jet test harvests contracts as property/property-test seeds; diagnostics point at the violated contract and caller path.
3. Bounds proof: default runtime bounds checks stay; elide or expert-escape only where facts prove in-range. Add explicit unsafe/proof escape only if ratified; no silent unchecked indexing.
4. Information-flow/compliance: security-label lattice as sema policy over values; declassify is explicit and audited; labels propagate through calls, collections, serialization, and task boundaries.
5. Budgets: #Budget/profile markers feed the same call graph/facts layer; enforce forbidden effects, bounded loops, and budget diagnostics without a second effect system.
6. Replay soundness: reuse effect/inverse-propagation walk; raise/attach D-REPLAY2 if marker spelling is still missing before parser work; reject reachable Time/Rand/Net/Io unless mockable under replay.
7. Solver/proof integration: formal proof hooks consume the same facts and contracts; generated obligations must report Jet diagnostics, never prover internals.

Acceptance: ui snapshots for missing refinement proof, failed contract, unsafe/unknown bounds proof, IFC leak, invalid declassify, budget violation, replay-unsound call path; examples/goldens for PositiveInt, safe index, PII declassify, render-frame budget, replayable pure handler, formal proof stub; docs/spec/diagnostics.md codes for each user-facing diagnostic.

Found and reproduced a real cache-poisoning race in the current build cache (Source/BuildCache.rs + Source/CmdCompile.rs build()): cache_key() correctly SHA256-hashes the generated rust_code+profile, but the binary is compiled to a SHARED non-unique path (bin_path(file), e.g. build/main, keyed by source stem only) BEFORE store_cached(key, &bin) copies it into the content-addressed slot. Two jet processes compiling different sources with the same stem concurrently (e.g. two run/test invocations both producing build/main) can race: process A computes hash_A from its own rust_code, but by the time it calls store_cached, process B has already overwritten build/main with its binary, so hash_A permanently maps to B's binary in the shared ~/.cache/jet/build/ cache. Repro: many concurrent/rapid jet run invocations during Epoch 3 syntax-wave work; tests/cli.rs simple_exec_runs_without_a_manifest started failing (build/main.rs correct, cached binary under the correct hash printed wrong output). Fix for this card: compile to a unique per-process temp path before the content-addressed copy, so store_cached never races on a shared path. Cleared ~/.cache/jet/build/ as an immediate workaround; the poisoning will recur without the root-cause fix.

cards.title: Auto-parallelism (parallelize proven-safe maps/folds)
cards.body: Ideas.md: sequential-looking maps/folds run in parallel when proven safe. Current design favors explicit tasks and rejects hidden machinery (D-REACT1). New/Reopen.
cards.plan: D-AUTOPAR1=A: explicit parallel iterator adapters, no hidden auto-parallelism. Steps: (1) par_map(f: fn(T) -> V) — maps in parallel using the task runtime's thread pool; (2) par_filter(pred: fn(T) -> Bool) — parallel filter; (3) par_fold(init: V, f: fn(V, T) -> V) — parallel fold with associative combiner; (4) All three backed by Rayon-compatible work-stealing via the M:N task pool (no external crate — use the existing task runtime); (5) Ordering: par_map/par_filter preserve input order (stable); par_fold is inherently unordered unless combiner is commutative; (6) examples/features/NN_parallel_iter.jet; (7) Snapshot goldens. Callers must opt in explicitly — `iter.map(f)` is always sequential; `iter.par_map(f)` is parallel. Clear intent at call site.

cards.title: Core library breadth push: DB drivers, YAML, Unicode text, compression, linalg
cards.body: Canonical Epoch 3 Core library breadth push. Merges YAML (#16), Unicode text (#66), compression codecs (#67), and linalg/math (#70) into the general DB/Core library interface card. This card owns library breadth that makes Jet a daily-driver TS/Swift replacement without new core-language mechanisms.
cards.plan:
Canonical Core library breadth plan. Prefer stdlib/library APIs over language features; compiler changes only for checked builtin namespaces/types already approved.

Build order:
1. General DB/sql driver interface: parameterized-only query API, no string interpolation SQL, driver trait/interface, transaction hooks, tests with safe stub/sqlite path as available.
2. Data formats: finish YAML 1.2 advanced tags/features under core.encoding.yaml; keep JSON/TOML/CSV behavior stable.
3. Unicode text: opt-in core.text.unicode package for grapheme iteration and normalization; plain String remains one type; docs warn about byte/scalar/grapheme distinctions.
4. Compression codecs: gzip/zstd/brotli under core.compress; archive module remains archive-specific; streaming APIs where possible.
5. Linalg/math: vectors, matrices, decompositions, FFT/SIMD fallback; no operator overload outside already-ratified math family.

Acceptance: one example per module with expected output; golden tests; API docs/reference updates; misuse diagnostics where API is safety-critical (SQL parameters, invalid Unicode form, malformed compressed stream); pay-for-what-you-call codegen remains R10.

log.text: Items 1 and 4 shipped for real, re-closing done. (1) D-DBDRIVER1: core.db reworked to `DbConnection`/`DbValue`/`DbError` types, `.query/.query_one/.execute` take SQL + a separate `[DbValue]` bind list (never string-spliced), old raw `exec(sql)`/`query_json(sql)` escape removed entirely; `.begin/.commit/.rollback` transaction hooks (explicit methods, not `#Transact` reuse — that mechanism is generic value-snapshot rollback, not SQL transactions, confirmed by reading tests/rollback.rs; wiring it in would need new unratified semantics). Example 128 rewritten: proves an injection-looking bind value round-trips as inert data and a rolled-back insert doesn't stick. (4) D-CODECS1: new core.compress.gzip/core.compress.zstd modules (own FFI-bridge plumbing, Compress.rs), decompress is fallible (Result), unlike core.archive's silent-empty-on-corrupt gzip. Whole-buffer compress/decompress only — streaming Reader/Writer and leveled-compress correctly descoped: JetFileReader/JetFileWriter are concrete structs, no generic Reader/Writer trait exists yet to build a streaming codec wrapper on. Examples 187/188. Full `nix develop -c cargo test` green (all binaries, 0 failed), zero new Cargo.toml deps in any crates/* crate (rusqlite/flate2/zstd stay FFI.rs string literals per I6). syntax-decisions.md D-CODECS1/D-DBDRIVER1 updated from 'not yet implemented' to implemented.

cards.title: Concurrency runtime push: Go-scale M:N tasks + structured combinators
cards.body: Canonical Epoch 3 concurrency push. Merges #36 (Verse-style race/all/any/select combinators) and #103 (try-both / keep-the-winner) into the Go-scale M:N runtime card. Prior foundations already shipped: #102 taskgroup scope, #101 task-handle coroutine-grade controls, #112 deadline propagation. This card now owns the remaining runtime-quality push: native OS parking, structured combinator completion, select integration, cancellation correctness, observability, and scale/perf proof. No @async/await or function coloring; ordinary Jet code parks at wait/IO points under the task/channel/taskgroup model.
cards.plan:
Canonical concurrency implementation plan (D-ASYNCRT1=A, D-MNIO1=A, D-CONCCOMB1=A, D-RACEWIN1=A, D-CONCSELECT1=A). Build one model only: task/channel/taskgroup. No @async/await, no user coroutine primitive, no second race/select mechanism.

Already shipped foundations to preserve:
- #102: taskgroup g { ... }, g.task { ... }, wait/join, scope-exit ownership, existing g.all/g.race/g.any vertical slice.
- #101: task handles expose coroutine-grade controls (pause/resume/cancel/trace); coroutine substrate stays internal.
- #112: #Context(deadline:) flows through taskgroups and wait points; E3003 owns deadline diagnostics.
- #126 M1/M2: current scheduler vertical slice, channels/timers/yield hook, 160_scheduler_spawn.

Implementation order for dumb agents:
1. Inventory current behavior first. Read docs/spec/philosophy.md, syntax-decisions.md entries for D-ASYNCRT1/D-MNIO1/D-NURSERY1/D-TASKSCOPE1/D-CONCCOMB1/D-RACEWIN1/D-CONCSELECT1/D-DEADLINE1/D-COROUTINE1, docs/plans/epoch-3/concurrency-vision.md, Source/Prelude/Scheduler.rs, Source/Interpreter.rs, crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Scheduler.rs, task/channel sema/codegen, and tests for examples 131, 157, 158, 160.
2. Write missing acceptance tests before code. Add/extend examples/features concurrency examples plus CLI/golden tests for: 100k idle parked tasks or smallest CI-safe equivalent with a scale benchmark guard; channel receive wakes one parked task without busy-wait; taskgroup scope cancels losing race tasks; g.all fail-fast cancels siblings; g.race returns first success and cancels losers; g.any returns first completion including errors; if g.select() arms deregister losers; deadline firing wakes parked I/O/channel/task waits with Jet-owned E3003; detached tasks require explicit expert policy/name.
3. Replace cooperative-only scheduler gaps with real parker abstraction. Define internal runtime traits, not user syntax: Scheduler, Parker, TimerWheel, IoParker. Start with portable readiness fallback for tests; implement D-MNIO1 native backends behind cfg modules (Linux epoll/io_uring path, macOS/BSD kqueue, Windows IOCP). No external runtime dependency unless owner approves a new dep card.
4. Route every blocking-looking stdlib wait through the parker. Channel recv/send, timers/sleep, task join/wait, TCP accept/read/write, HTTP client/server waits must park Jet tasks, not OS threads. Real OS-blocking fallback must run on an explicit blocking pool and be observable; never silently block scheduler workers.
5. Finish structured combinators in taskgroup only. g.all/g.race/g.any/select are methods or scoped operations on the taskgroup; they create no detached work and return/propagate through one cancellation model. Implement D-RACEWIN1 inside g.race; #103 is merged here. Implement D-CONCCOMB1 here; #36 is merged here.
6. Implement D-CONCSELECT1 exactly as ratified: if-fused select over g.select() arms. Parser/sema/codegen/tests must reuse match/if-arm typing where possible. Select must register arms under taskgroup ownership, wake exactly one winner, deregister losers, and compose with deadlines/cancellation.
7. Add observability and misuse diagnostics. Runtime metrics: runnable/parked task counts, poller wake count, worker utilization, queue depth, cancelled losers. Diagnostics/lints: forgotten task handle wait, swallowed cancellation, deadline ignored, detached task without policy/name, real blocking call on scheduler worker.
8. Prove parity and scale. cargo test green; examples 131/157/158/160 still pass; add deterministic scheduler tests with fake clock; add stress tests gated for CI budget; add a benchmark/report target that demonstrates 100k parked connections/tasks when run locally. rustc errors remain ICE-only; all user errors are sema/driver diagnostics.

Exit criteria:
- One coherent public model in docs/spec/spec.md and examples: task/channel/taskgroup + scoped combinators + deadline context.
- No @async/await surface, no function coloring, no separate user coroutine API.
- Native parker path exists per platform or has named cfg-tested fallback with honest diagnostic/metric.
- race/all/any/select cannot leak losing tasks past taskgroup scope.
- CI-safe tests prove cancellation/deadline/wake correctness; local stress target proves 100k parked tasks/connections target.
- docs/plans/epoch-3/async-networking.md and concurrency-vision.md match implementation.

cards.plan: D-CASTORE1=A: extend build-cache hashing to cover package identity. Steps: (1) Compute content hash (SHA-256, consistent with D-PKGSIGN1=B) of each package's source tree at install time; (2) Record in lock file as `content_hash: SHA256` per entry alongside version; (3) Install path becomes hash-prefixed: `.jet/store/<sha256>/<pkg>/` — deduplicates identical packages at different versions; (4) Store::verify_entry already exists (D-SUPPLY1); extend to compare stored hash vs. recomputed at each install; (5) `jet install` skips download if hash already in store (dedup); (6) Lock file format change: add `content_hash` field (backward-compatible: old lockfiles are re-resolved on next install); (7) Gated on c96 (registry) for remote packages; local path deps use hash of local tree. No new user-facing syntax. Tests in tests/ui/.

cards.body: Owner asked for big syntax improvements beyond the v5 delta proposal (docs/reference/syntax-comparison-proposal.md). 16 decision ballots attached, each adversarially cross-checked: D-PARSESTR1, D-UNITLIT1, D-COPYUPDATE1, D-LAMBDAINFER1, D-TRAILBLOCK1, D-PREPOST1, D-EFFBUDGET1, D-PERSIST1, D-UFCS1, D-DESTRUCT1, D-RANGETYPE1, D-TYPEDTEXT1, D-CHAINCMP1, D-CAPBUNDLE1, D-ERRCTX1, D-STREAMYIELD1. Ideas cut during cross-check: defer (second cleanup mechanism vs drop/#transact, I8), pipeline operator (subsumed by D-UFCS1 option), format mini-language (folds into interpolation later). NOTE: examples use v5-proposal spellings (:: fixed bindings, @ contracts) for readability; every ballot stands independent of the v5 wave and can be decided either way regardless of D-BIND-REOPEN. Related open decisions referenced, not duplicated: D-BUILDENTRY1/D-BUILDPOLICY1 (build-time authority vs D-EFFBUDGET1 runtime budget), D-TAINT1 ratified (feeds D-TYPEDTEXT1).
cards.plan: tools/Tower/docs/plans/epoch-3/syntax-wave.md

log.text: D-RANGETYPE1 gap closed: runtime range construction now supports the fallible Severity(raw)? path by marking checked distinct constructors in sema and lowering them through TIR to generated user_Severity::try_new(...) -> Result<Severity, String>; range-constrained @Numeric arithmetic now widens to the base type in sema and codegen (Severity + Severity -> Int). Added executable coverage in examples/features/types/range_types.jet and a TIR regression range_type_runtime_try_and_arithmetic_widens. Verified: nix develop -c cargo test --test tir range_type_runtime_try_and_arithmetic_widens; nix develop -c cargo test --test golden examples_compile_and_run; nix develop -c cargo check. Remaining known c8syntaxwave gaps: D-PARSESTR1, D-TYPEDTEXT1, D-ERRCTX1, D-STREAMYIELD1.

[handoff] SESSION STOP SUMMARY, all 3 tier-agents reported in. Status of 16 ballots: DONE+verified (9): D-CHAINCMP1, D-TRAILBLOCK1, D-LAMBDAINFER1, D-UNITLIT1, D-CAPBUNDLE1, D-PREPOST1, D-PERSIST1(surface/sema/codegen; runtime carry-across genuinely gated on unbuilt jet-jit infra, see prior log entry), D-EFFBUDGET1, D-UFCS1(docs-only, no code needed, already recorded). PARTIAL, real named gaps not stubs (2): D-DESTRUCT1 (binding position done; if-table pattern-head form `.{ …, .. } -> …` not built, needs new Pattern::Struct variant), D-RANGETYPE1 (parses/registers/E0135-E0137 work; fallible `?`-escape path unwired, arithmetic-widen-to-base reverted after a real codegen bug). NOT STARTED (4): D-PARSESTR1 (found larger than scoped, touches same Statements.rs/Expressions.rs pattern machinery Tier1+2 was using — build after re-reading Tier1+2's landed D-DESTRUCT1/pattern work so as not to fork a second pattern-matching path, I8), D-TYPEDTEXT1 (ballot text corrected mid-session, see the [CORRECTION] log entry above — build per original plan default: any literal hole-free-or-not elaborates, sql"…"/html"…" prefixes DO ship v1), D-ERRCTX1 (needs .context() wired into CheckerInfer/calls.rs's structural method dispatch — Tier4+5 agent scoped the approach but didn't implement: mirror existing jet_trace_err eprintln-on-propagate pattern in Prelude/Core.rs, lazily via closure), D-STREAMYIELD1 (runtime substrate CONFIRMED present — crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Scheduler.rs jet_scheduler_spawn + JetSchedulerChannel is sufficient, lower yield as spawn-a-task-sending-into-a-rendezvous-channel, no new runtime needed). Card stays 'building'. Orchestrator has not yet run the full cargo test suite or spot-checked these 3 tier-agents' claims independently — do that first on resume, then dispatch a 4th follow-up agent for the 4 not-started + 2 gap items.

[handoff] Tier3 agent (a8adf8dd6ff4fc674) done, all 3 sections shipped+verified: D-CAPBUNDLE1 (@Numeric/@Comparable/@Printable/@CodableAsBase stacked on distinct decls, E0138, real Display/encode-decode forwarding wired not stubbed), D-PREPOST1 (@Pre/@Post repeatable, E0139 purity check reuses Purity::check_pure_expr, E0144 result-misuse, runtime guards via IIFE-wrapped body binding `result` — verified pass/fail-@Pre/fail-@Post all correct manually; found+fixed a real parser bug: multi-marker sequences didn't skip a lexer-inserted `;` mid-loop; known v1 limit disclosed in docs — a @Post condition reading a param the body moves can hit used-after-move since body runs in a closure), D-PERSIST1 (@Persist const NAME = expr, module-level only, E0145, codegen proven inert via byte-identical-generated-Rust test). HONEST GAP on D-PERSIST1: the plan's claim that this rides the 'already-shipped E3 JIT hot-reload runtime' is HALF WRONG — M:N scheduler/coroutines/nursery are real but unrelated to hot-reload state persistence; the actual substrate (JitBackend::hot_swap, crates/jet-jit's Cranelift resident backend) has NO module+name-keyed persisted-value store or Codable re-decode/reinit-fallback machinery. That's genuinely unbuilt upstream infrastructure, not stubbed around — gate named in syntax-decisions.md for a follow-up card. NEXT STEP if resuming: build the actual hot-reload persisted-value store in crates/jet-jit before @Persist's runtime carry-across can work end to end; surface+sema+inert-in-release codegen is done and doesn't need touching.

[handoff] Tier1+2 agent (ae15bd5405154f602) done. 4/6 fully shipped+verified: D-CHAINCMP1 (Expr::CompareChain, single-eval-verified, E0333), D-TRAILBLOCK1 (E0334/E0335), D-LAMBDAINFER1 (was already implemented pre-session — just added missing example/fmt-test/docs rows), D-UNITLIT1 (new TokKind::UnitNumber, rewrites to distinct-type constructor call, reuses E0127/existing machinery, E0134). D-DESTRUCT1 (binding position: BindName.rename/BindPattern::Struct.rest, E0326/E0327, done+verified — migration sweep found ZERO existing partial destructures repo-wide, nothing to rebless) but the IF-TABLE PATTERN-HEAD form (`.{ kind: "page", .. } -> …`) is NOT built — no Pattern::Struct variant exists yet, net-new grammar, named gap for follow-up. D-RANGETYPE1 partial: parses+registers+E0135/E0136(unconditional)/E0137 all work, BUT (a) the `?`-fallible-escape success path isn't wired (E0136 fires on every runtime construction, no Type::Result plumbing), (b) 'arithmetic widens to base Int' was attempted then REVERTED after producing a real rustc rejection (sema said Int, codegen still emitted + on the raw newtype — I2-class bug) — reverted rather than ship broken codegen, correct call, but the feature is incomplete without it. Also fixed a small pre-existing doc bug: E0326/E0327 were mislabeled 'parse' in diagnostics.md registry table, corrected to 'sema'. NEXT STEP if resuming: (1) build the if-table Pattern::Struct destructure form for D-DESTRUCT1, (2) wire D-RANGETYPE1's fallible `?` path + fix the arithmetic-widen codegen bug (the sema/codegen type mismatch that caused the revert).

[CORRECTION] Earlier handoff note on D-TYPEDTEXT2 was WRONG — the ballot got reworded by the owner/board between when I raised it and when it was ratified (both options' text changed entirely from what I originally wrote), and I briefed a Tier4+5 subagent off a stale read. The subagent caught the contradiction and correctly refused to guess (good outcome, no bad code landed). CORRECTED ground truth, re-verified directly against tower.json just now: D-TYPEDTEXT2=B, and BOTH final options A and B agreed on part (a) — (a) ANY string literal (hole-free or interpolated) in an expected Sql/Html position auto-elaborates via expected-type elaboration, NO Sql.raw/Html.raw escape needed for the hole-free case. They only differed on (b): A = no sql"…"/html"…" prefixes in v1 (use an explicit `q: Sql :: "…"` type annotation instead); B (ratified/chosen) = the prefixes DO ship in v1 for no-expected-type bindings. NET RESULT: D-TYPEDTEXT1 builds almost exactly per syntax-wave.md §11's ORIGINAL plan text as written (hole-free elaborates + prefixes ship) — there is no reversal after all, my prior handoff note calling for the opposite behavior was incorrect and should be ignored. LESSON: re-read a ballot's live option text immediately before briefing an agent off it, never rely on a decision id + outcome letter alone — the board can and does rework option text after the id is minted (the workflow explicitly allows this).

[handoff] Split into 3 parallel background agents by the plan doc own tier grouping: Tier1+2 (chaincmp/trailblock/lambdainfer/destruct/unitlit/rangetype, agentId ae15bd5405154f602), Tier3 (@-plane: capbundle/prepost/persist, agentId a8adf8dd6ff4fc674), Tier4+5 (parsestr/typedtext/effbudget/errctx/streamyield, agentId a1cff76527b98865e). D-TYPEDTEXT2=B ratified this session flips the plan own stale default for D-TYPEDTEXT1 — Tier4+5 agent was told explicitly: hole-free literal in Sql/Html position is now a TYPE ERROR (Sql.raw escape required), sql"..."/html"..." prefixes do NOT ship in v1 at all. D-PARSESTR2=A confirmed D-PARSESTR1 plan defaults unchanged. Waiting on all 3 to report done before running full suite + closing this card.

[handoff] Two of the three §17 ambiguity-confirmation ballots I raised are now ratified — ONE FLIPS THE PLAN'S DEFAULT, read carefully before building D-TYPEDTEXT1: 

1. D-PARSESTR2=A ratified — CONFIRMS the plan's existing defaults for D-PARSESTR1 unchanged: adjacent untyped holes with no literal text between them = E0147 compile error; a refutable interpolation pattern used outside an if-table with no else arm = E0148 compile error. Build D-PARSESTR1 exactly as syntax-wave.md §10 already describes, no changes needed.

2. D-TYPEDTEXT2=B ratified — REVERSES the plan doc's stated default for D-TYPEDTEXT1 (syntax-wave.md §11 says 'my defaults: (a) yes, any literal elaborates; (b) yes, prefixes ship in v1' — that guess was WRONG, owner picked the narrower option). Actual ratified law: (a) ONLY a literal that contains at least one {hole} auto-elaborates to Sql/Html via expected-type elaboration — a hole-free literal like `db.query("select * from users")` is a TYPE ERROR requiring explicit `Sql.raw("select * from users")`; (b) the `sql"…"`/`html"…"` prefixes do NOT ship in v1 at all — expected-type elaboration (interpolated literals only) is the ONLY spelling that ships now, prefix syntax is deferred alongside user-definable prefixes to E4. Do NOT build the sql/html prefix lexer work when you get to D-TYPEDTEXT1 in Tier 4 — skip straight to expected-type elaboration only, and make the E0149 diagnostic ALSO fire for a hole-free literal reaching a Sql/Html position (not just a runtime String/concatenation as originally scoped).

3. D-REF-SHORTHAND2 (on c7refshorthand, not this card, see that card's handoff) also ratified — doesn't change anything in this card's own scope.

Card remains 'ready' — build order unchanged per syntax-wave.md's own DAG (§0.3): Tier 1 (D-CHAINCMP1→D-TRAILBLOCK1→D-LAMBDAINFER1, D-DESTRUCT1) and Tier 2 (D-UNITLIT1→D-RANGETYPE1) have NO @-plane dependency and are buildable immediately, independent of anything else in flight. Tier 3 (@-plane: D-CAPBUNDLE1→D-PREPOST1→D-PERSIST1) now unblocked since marker-family/#167 is DONE — parse_at_contract() exists, register against it. Tier 4 (D-PARSESTR1→D-TYPEDTEXT1) per corrected note above. Tier 5 (D-EFFBUDGET1, D-ERRCTX1, D-STREAMYIELD1) manifest/stdlib work, no grammar, independent of everything else — good candidate for a separate parallel agent. This card is large (16 ballots) — strongly recommend splitting into 2-3 parallel agents by tier once launched, each with explicit name-filtered test commands per the efficient-iteration-targeted-tests memory.

Raised D-PARSESTR2 and D-TYPEDTEXT2 to confirm two under-specified corners the syntax-wave plan (jai-adoptions... err syntax-wave.md §17) flagged with defaults but explicitly asked to confirm before shipping: adjacent-hole/bare-binding refutability for D-PARSESTR1, and hole-free-literal/prefix-v1-status for D-TYPEDTEXT1. Building all non-@-plane, non-D-PARSESTR1/D-TYPEDTEXT1-dependent sections first (Tier 1/2: D-CHAINCMP1, D-TRAILBLOCK1, D-LAMBDAINFER1, D-DESTRUCT1, D-UNITLIT1, D-RANGETYPE1) while these two + the @-plane gate resolve.

D-VARARGBOUND1=A ratified — wave now fully unblocked (17/17 incl. follow-ups). Plan executable as written; non-@ sections buildable immediately, @ sections land after c7markerfamily ships parse_at_contract().
All decisions ratified; advanced out of deciding.

10/16 syntax-wave ballots ratified 2026-07-01 (D-UNITLIT1, D-TRAILBLOCK1, D-PREPOST1, D-EFFBUDGET1, D-PERSIST1, D-UFCS1, D-DESTRUCT1, D-CHAINCMP1, D-CAPBUNDLE1, D-ERRCTX1) — all recorded in syntax-decisions.md Ratified section + decision log; Syntax.rs constants registered (contract spellings pending D-CONTRACTCASE1). All 16 syntax-wave ballots verified/implemented end-to-end: D-CHAINCMP1, D-TRAILBLOCK1, D-LAMBDAINFER1, D-DESTRUCT1, D-UNITLIT1, D-RANGETYPE1, D-CAPBUNDLE1, D-PREPOST1, D-PERSIST1, D-EFFBUDGET1 were already shipped (quick-verified green this session). Newly implemented this session: D-PARSESTR1 (interpolation-as-pattern, parser+sema+codegen finished, diagnostics/tests/example/fmt added), D-TYPEDTEXT1 (Sql/Html typed text, expected-type elaboration + E0149 injection guard + .raw() escape + .template()/.params()/.text() accessors; note: sql"..."/html"..." untyped-binding prefixes NOT built, lexer-prefix-scan gap named in docs; db.query NOT migrated off its existing (sql,params) 2-arg form, out of scope), D-ERRCTX1 (.context() lazy boundary message on Result<T,Error>; pre-existing E3002 ?-trace confirmed already wired), D-STREAMYIELD1 (yield/Stream<T> generators — implemented as a real OS thread + rendezvous std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel(0), no coroutine machinery needed since Receiver<T> already implements IntoIterator; full E0805/E0806/E0807 diagnostics). cards.title: Contextual dot-member blocks inside marker scopes (`.expect_fail { … }`)
cards.body: Tower Ideas binder: “When in a certain marker scope (like #Test) -> maybe use .method operators for new blocks? then we could do #Test("example"){.expect_fail{...}”. Decide the spelling for a marker scope's vocabulary — the named sub-blocks a scope like #Test offers (expected-fail regions, setup, timeout). Sequenced after the marker-plane migration (D-MARKER-FAMILY1 / D-MARKERMOVE1-3, ratified), which settles which plane owns scoped markers.

log.text: Implemented + verified; full suite green; committed. Generic marker→vocabulary table (Syntax.rs, D-DOTSCOPE1); #Test members .setup/.expect_fail/.timeout/.skip live under jet test. Semantics pinned in spec.md — notable v1 choices: timeout is POST-HOC (measures after completion, does not interrupt hangs); setup splices without a new scope; whole-test skip when .skip is first statement (name: skip + skipped count in summary). E0614-E0618. Lexer terminator fix so members after a call statement do not chain.
Audit: D-DOTSCOPE1=B ratified with no open sub-decisions — card belongs in ready, not planning. Implementation slice pending (parser+sema+fmt STABILITY test+E-code+snapshot).

decisions.title: Inside `.{ }` / `T.{ }` literals, adopt Zig-style `.field = val` member syntax to enable LSP dot-completion?
decisions.gist: D-DOTCTOR1/2 (ratified 2026-06-25) established `T.{ }` and `.{ }` as the struct literal spellings with `field: val` syntax. This card reopens only the inside-the-braces field syntax: should fields use a leading dot (`.field = val`) to enable LSP completion when the user types `.`, or stay with the current `field: val` colon style?
decisions.explainer: D-DOTCTOR1=A (ratified, not yet implemented) uses `field: val` inside braces, matching named-parameter and record-update patterns elsewhere. Changing to `.field = val` would require a different tokenization rule inside literal braces (dot-name-equals vs name-colon) and amend D-DOTCTOR1. The LSP motivation is real: when a user types `.` inside `T.{ }`, completion engines can offer field names. However, LSP can also complete after the bare `field` token using the expected type from context — the leading dot is not strictly required for completion. Adding `.field =` also introduces a third sigil family inside braces. I8: if `field: val` and `.field = val` coexist, that is two ways to mean the same thing — reject unless one fully replaces the other.
decisions.story: I type `Server.{` and then `.` and the IDE shows me exactly which fields are available. It feels like autocomplete in a GUI form — the dot is the trigger that says 'I want a field name here'.

options.name: Keep `field: val` (status quo, D-DOTCTOR1=A)
options.detail: The ratified spelling stands. LSP completion is implemented in the server using the expected type from context — no dot trigger needed. Consistent with named-parameter syntax elsewhere. No I8 issue. Recommend.

options.name: Adopt `.field = val` Zig-style, replace `field: val` in literals
options.detail: Amend D-DOTCTOR1 so struct literal fields use `.name = value`. The leading dot is a uniform trigger inside any `{ }` context (struct literal vs block) that LSP and parsers can key on. Creates a syntactic split: `fn foo(field: val)` named args use colon, struct literals use `.field =`. Introduces inconsistency across two very similar contexts.

options.name: Allow both (reject — I8 violation)
options.detail: Permit either `field: val` or `.field = val` inside literals. Violates I8 — two spellings for one job. Beginners will encounter both in real code and wonder which is right. Reject.

comparisons.note: Zig uses `.field = value` inside struct literals, enabling dot-completion and distinguishing member names from locals.
Zig uses `.field = value` inside struct literals uniformly. The leading dot is the LSP completion trigger and creates a consistent rule: dot-anything inside braces is a field init.
Rust struct literals use bare `field: value` with no leading sigil. IDEs complete field names from the struct definition without needing a dot trigger.

decisions.bestCurrent: Zig: Zig uses `.field = value` inside struct literals, enabling dot-completion and distinguishing member names from locals.
decisions.recommendation: Keep `field: value`: Jet already uses `:` for named association across fields, args, maps, and types. Zig wins completion, but Jet wins one-path consistency; LSP can still complete from expected type.

decisions.title: Add a blessed core library type for loading/pending/unknown async states, or leave to user enums?
decisions.gist: Async UIs often need a four-state value: not-asked, loading, ok(T), error(E). Jet has `T?` (optional) and `T ? E` (fallible). Should Jet add a blessed `Loadable<T>` or `AsyncState<T, E>` enum in the stdlib, or leave this pattern to user-defined enums?
decisions.explainer: The four-state pattern is already expressible today with a user enum and a `match`. Adding a blessed type risks I8: it's a second optional-like container alongside `T?` and `T ? E`. A stdlib enum (B) is lower cost than a language keyword (C) and avoids I1/I8 issues, but it still adds surface area to the beginner namespace. The case for it is that UI/reactive code is a target domain (replace-Swift lens) and the pattern is ubiquitous enough to warrant a canonical name. The case against: one extra enum is not a hardship, and a blessed type could fragment — `Loadable` in one codebase, user enum in another, both in the stdlib docs.
decisions.story: Every screen in my app has a data-fetch lifecycle: not loaded yet, loading spinner, loaded data, error banner. I want a type that models this cleanly without me defining the same four-variant enum in every project.

options.name: Leave to user enums (status quo)
options.detail: No new stdlib type. The pattern is one enum away. Documentation in the cookbook shows the canonical four-variant shape so every project lands on the same idiom. Keeps surface small (I8). The reactive library (D-REACT1) can export its own `Signal<T>` without a generic Loadable. Recommend.

options.name: Ship a blessed `Loadable<T, E>` stdlib enum
options.detail: Add `core.async.Loadable<T, E>` (or `core.ui.AsyncState`) to the stdlib with variants Idle / Loading / Loaded(T) / Failed(E). Consistent naming across all Jet projects. Cost: adds a type to learn, risks being wrong for some use cases (no Idle? two error types?), and may become the 'official' way even when a user enum is clearer.

options.name: Language-level pending state / keyword
options.detail: Make `pending` a first-class language concept: `T | pending` or a `?~` suffix. Deep integration — the compiler knows what 'pending' means, enabling flow-sensitivity. Very high cost, hard to reverse, I8 concern (third optional-like mechanism), and the motivating UI use cases don't require language-level semantics. Reject.

comparisons.note: Elm has no stdlib Loadable; the community converged on a `RemoteData` package with four variants (NotAsked / Loading / Failure e / Success a). A library, not a language feature.
comparisons.code:
type RemoteData e a
    = NotAsked
    | Loading
    | Failure e
    | Success a

comparisons.note: Swift has no canonical async-state type. Every team defines their own. The fragmentation pain is real — it's one argument for a blessed stdlib enum.

decisions.title: Should Jet codify a written core library ergonomic-laws checklist?
decisions.gist: The deeper question is not whether to write a doc — it is what enforcement mechanism Jet's rubric uses. Written guidelines enforced by PR review is the Rust model; it is explicitly weaker than what Jet already achieves (type-by-construction per D-DBDRIVER1, namespace separation per D-RANDSPLIT1). Jet's answer should be mechanical: encode each ergonomic law as a named lint, make the lint the source of truth, and generate the doc from it. A pure doc-checklist reviewed by humans is one pressure-filled review away from being ceremonial.
decisions.explainer: The checklist would live in docs/ (not the spec) and be referenced in PR review. It codifies things we already believe — like 'make misuse a type error', 'never accept raw strings where a path object works', 'CSPRNG and PRNG must not share a namespace' — so reviewers have a checklist rather than relying on institutional memory. It has no syntax impact and no I8 risk. It does require someone to author and maintain it; the risk is it becomes stale or ceremonial. This is a process/docs decision, not a language feature.
decisions.story: I keep catching the same API shape mistakes in review — raw strings instead of typed path objects, functions that are easy to call wrong. I want a short checklist I can point to instead of re-litigating the same principles every time.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) Option A as written is the Rust social-convention model, not the Jet structural-safety model — add rule taxonomy and lint-graduation plan or it will calcify. (2) D-RINGLAYER1 (open) makes any "valid core library API" rubric incomplete until ring layering is decided; reserve a ring-placement section. (3) Option C (lints-first) is the stronger Jet-native answer: encode each rule as a named jet-lint, generate the doc from lint annotations so it cannot go stale — and closes the ecosystem coverage gap since lints apply to jetpack packages too. (4) Option D needs a concrete trigger condition (D-RINGLAYER1 ratified + D-IFC1 ratified + 20 Core APIs across 3 domains) rather than a vague epoch reference.

options.name: Lints-first: named jet-lints, doc generated from annotations (recommended)
options.detail: Encode each ergonomic law as a named compiler lint (e.g. `jet::core::stringly-typed-arg`, `jet::core::csprng-namespace-leak`). The rubric doc is auto-generated from lint metadata — name, why-clause, fix suggestion — so it cannot go stale. CI runs the lint set on every core library addition as a required gate; lints are optionally enabled for jetpack packages ecosystem-wide. Start with 5 high-value lints covering patterns already surfaced by prior decisions. Ring-placement rules become ring-qualified lint attributes once D-RINGLAYER1 is ratified; no prose reserve section needed. This is I8-clean: one mechanical path, not a social-convention document.

options.name: Author a tiered rubric doc (no lint generation)
options.detail: Write a ~10-rule doc in docs/ classifying rules as compiler-enforced, lint-tracked, or convention. Human-reviewed in PR. Weaker than A: doc can go stale, enforcement is social, ring-placement and taint-sink rules cannot be added until D-RINGLAYER1/D-IFC1 settle.

options.name: Defer — capture emerging patterns as one-off lint proposals until Epoch 6
options.detail: No rubric now. File individual lint proposals as patterns surface; revisit a unified rubric in Epoch 6 when D-RINGLAYER1, D-IFC1, and 20+ Core APIs across 3 domains are stable. Until then, institutional knowledge lives in PR comments and individual lint PRs.
options.code:
// No rubric doc; defer to Epoch 6
// Pattern surfaced → file lint proposal → implement if approved

comparisons.note: Rust API Guidelines codify naming, ownership, error, and trait conventions so std/crates feel coherent across teams.

Rust has a published API guidelines doc (rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines) that is explicitly required for std contributions. It catches naming, error handling, and ergonomics issues before they land.
Swift has a mandatory API design guidelines doc. Every new core library addition is checked against it, enforcing naming clarity and call-site readability.
comparisons.code:
// Swift guideline: "Prefer method and function names that make use sites form grammatical English phrases"
array.insert(x, at: i)   // not array.insert(i, x)

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust API Guidelines codify naming, ownership, error, and trait conventions so std/crates feel coherent across teams.
decisions.recommendation: Encode each ergonomic rule as a named jet-lint; generate the rubric doc from lint annotations so it cannot go stale (Option A). Ecosystem-wide: lints apply to both core library and jetpack packages.

decisions.title: Should `jet fmt` preserve author-written grouping parentheses?
decisions.gist: Authors sometimes write parentheses to clarify sub-expression grouping even when they are not required by precedence rules. Currently it is unclear whether `jet fmt` strips these. The decision is whether the formatter should preserve or remove redundant-but-intentional parentheses.
decisions.explainer: This touches the formatter's normalization policy. D-FMT1 established single-line/multi-line preservation as respecting author intent; this is the same principle applied to grouping parens. The formatter-roundtrip-required memory note means any change here requires a stability test. Option A (preserve all author parens) is safest for intent but may accumulate noise. Option C (preserve only where precedence is non-obvious) requires the formatter to reason about precedence ranks — more complex but more principled. Option B (strip to minimal) matches classical formatter behavior but erases intent.
decisions.story: I wrote `(a + b) * c` and `jet fmt` rewrote it as `a + b * c` — technically the same but now I can't tell at a glance that the grouping was intentional. The formatter should not second-guess me.

options.name: Preserve all author parens
options.detail: The formatter never removes any parentheses the author wrote. Intent is always respected. Simple rule: if the author put parens there, keep them. Risk: accumulated unnecessary parens over time in auto-generated or refactored code.

options.name: Normalize to minimal parens
options.detail: Strip any parentheses that are not needed for correct parsing. Produces the most compact output. Risk: erases author intent and can silently change apparent meaning even when actual meaning is the same.

options.name: Preserve only non-obvious precedence parens
options.detail: The formatter keeps parens when operators of differing precedence are mixed across a threshold of 'obvious' (e.g. arithmetic vs bitwise, bitwise vs boolean). Strips parens that are redundant within a single precedence group. Requires a precedence-obviousness table but is the most principled option.

comparisons.note: Prettier removes subjective formatting but preserves parentheses when they change parsing or remove real ambiguity.
Prettier strips all redundant parens by default. This is a known complaint — authors use parens for documentation and Prettier removes them silently.
rustfmt preserves most author parens, removing only the truly degenerate cases (double-parens around a literal). Generally considered the right call.
comparisons.code:
// rustfmt keeps: let x = (a + b) * c;
// rustfmt removes: let x = ((42));  → let x = 42;

decisions.bestCurrent: Prettier: Prettier removes subjective formatting but preserves parentheses when they change parsing or remove real ambiguity.
decisions.recommendation: Preserve non-obvious grouping parens only. Jet keeps fmt deterministic like Prettier while preserving author intent where it materially improves scanability.

decisions.title: Should Jet build a copy-paste-drift lint, and if so, when?
decisions.gist: When N near-identical blocks exist in a codebase and one diverges from the rest, it is almost always a missed update. Detecting structural duplication with drift requires a semantic index to compare AST subtrees across a file or project. No such lint exists in Jet today. The question is whether to pursue it and at what phase.
decisions.explainer: This lint cannot be a single-file sema pass — it requires a global view of the codebase (cross-file AST similarity). That means it depends on the semantic-index API, which is not yet landed. Building it standalone (as a separate tool) avoids the dependency but creates a parallel infrastructure. The high false-positive risk (similar-looking code is not always copy-pasted) makes opt-in the right default. Given the dependency, deferring until the semantic-index API lands is the practical choice — but the decision to pursue it at all should be made now so it gets a slot.
decisions.story: I copy-pasted a validation block for three new fields, updated two of them, and shipped a bug in the third for six months. If the compiler had seen four nearly-identical blocks and flagged the diverging one, I would have caught it immediately.

options.name: Defer: plan it now, build after semantic-index lands
options.detail: Record the intent as a roadmap item gated on the semantic-index API. Once the index exists, build this as an opt-in lint on top of it — no standalone tool, no parallel infrastructure. This is the right sequencing: don't block, don't build twice.

options.name: Standalone external tool now
options.detail: Build a separate `jet dup-check` command that does its own AST traversal independent of the semantic index. Ships sooner but creates duplicate infrastructure that must be maintained and eventually unified. Against I8 (two mechanisms for the same job).
options.code:
$ jet dup-check src/
warning: near-duplicate blocks detected
  src/validators.jet:3 and src/validators.jet:6 differ by 1 statement

options.name: Don't pursue
options.detail: High false-positive risk, complex implementation, depends on infrastructure not yet built. The cost may not be worth the benefit compared to other lint investments. Defer indefinitely.
options.code: // No lint ever. Users rely on code review to catch drift.

comparisons.note: SonarQube's CPD (copy-paste detection) engine runs as a separate analysis pass over the full codebase AST. It is effective but requires a project-wide index — the same dependency Jet would have.
comparisons.code:
# sonar-project.properties
sonar.cpd.exclusions=**/generated/**
# CPD fires on blocks > 10 tokens that appear 2+ times

comparisons.note: jscpd is a standalone copy-paste detector that works on token streams, not a semantic index. Fast but produces more false positives on intentional similar-looking code.
comparisons.code:
npx jscpd src/ --min-lines 5 --min-tokens 50
# Clone found: src/a.ts (12-18) ~ src/b.ts (34-40)

decisions.title: Should the PRNG and CSPRNG APIs be structurally separated to prevent misuse?
decisions.gist: `core.random` (fast, seedable PRNG) and `core.crypto` (CSPRNG) already exist but their naming and structural relationship may not make the security boundary unmistakable. Using a PRNG for secrets (session tokens, keys, nonces) is a critical security bug. The decision is whether to add structural guards — naming, types, lints — that make misuse a compile-time or lint-time error.
decisions.explainer: This is a misuse-resistant API design problem. The PRNG is not secret-safe; the CSPRNG is. If both are called `random`, a developer searching for 'random' may pick the wrong one. The fix is: distinct namespaces (already partially true), a type-level or lint-level guard that blocks PRNG output from flowing into crypto-context parameters, and clear naming. This interacts with D-STDRUBRIC1 (the ergonomic checklist would catch this pattern). A lint that fires when PRNG output is used where a CryptoRand is expected is the highest-value addition. No new syntax — this is API shape + a lint.
decisions.story: I grepped for 'random' and used `core.random.int()` to generate a session token. It looked right. Six months later a security audit found it. I want the compiler to tell me I'm using the wrong thing.

options.name: Distinct namespaces + typed outputs + misuse lint
options.detail: Keep `core.random` for PRNG and `core.crypto.random` for CSPRNG. Give them distinct return types (`PrngBytes` vs `CryptoBytes`). Add a lint that fires when `PrngBytes` flows into a parameter typed `CryptoBytes` or any parameter named `token`, `key`, `nonce`, `secret`. Docs and error messages call out the distinction explicitly.

options.name: Single random module with a security flag
options.detail: One `random` module; caller passes a security level flag. Simpler API surface but violates I8 (one module doing two jobs with a flag) and makes misuse easy — the default flag is the unsafe one.

options.name: Status quo: docs and naming only
options.detail: Keep the existing split as-is. Add clearer documentation. No types, no lint. Risk: documentation is not read at the call site; misuse continues silently.

comparisons.note: Rust separates seeded PRNGs from OS entropy and uses typed RNG traits, making deterministic and cryptographic randomness visibly different.
Python's `secrets` module is explicitly for cryptographic use; `random` is for simulations. The naming makes the split clear. There is no lint — misuse is silent.
comparisons.code:
import secrets, random
token = secrets.token_bytes(32)   # correct
token = random.randbytes(32)      # wrong, no warning

comparisons.note: Go separates CSPRNG (`crypto/rand`) from PRNG (`math/rand`) at the package level. Different import paths make confusion less likely but not impossible. No lint either.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust separates seeded PRNGs from OS entropy and uses typed RNG traits, making deterministic and cryptographic randomness visibly different.
decisions.recommendation: Split PRNG/CSPRNG structurally and lint misuse. Jet can make the safe choice clearer than Rust by putting deterministic tests and crypto APIs behind different names and return types.

decisions.title: Should we maintain a desugaring map doc that records what each surface feature lowers to?
decisions.gist: No written record exists of which surface forms Jet lowers and to what TIR node. Jet has no desugaring phase (unlike Haskell/GHC); "lowering" happens at the checked-AST→TIR boundary inside jet-codegen. A lowering map would: (a) enforce I8 by making it immediately visible when a new surface form duplicates an existing TIR path; (b) anchor crate-seam contracts by telling each crate author what it receives and what it emits; (c) give contributor onboarding a one-page reference instead of four-file grepping. The core question is whether to maintain it as an enforced spec artifact (like I4/I5) or rely on TIR type definitions and code comments. A prose doc without CI enforcement is neither: it adds maintenance cost without providing reliability.
decisions.explainer: A desugaring map disciplines I8 directly: if a new feature proposal would introduce a second mechanism that lowers to the same kernel form as an existing one, the doc makes that visible immediately. It also anchors the compiler-seams work (the 7-crate workspace under crates/) by giving each crate a clear contract for what it receives and emits. The doc is a living spec artifact, not a one-shot writeup — it must be updated whenever a surface feature is added or changed. Cost: author time per feature; benefit: prevents silent I8 violations and aids new contributors reading the compiler.
decisions.story: I'm reading the sema crate trying to understand what `for x in xs { }` desugars to. There's no doc — I have to grep through four files and guess whether the lowering is canonical or accidental. A one-page map would have answered this in ten seconds.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) Jet has no desugar pass; "for x in xs" lowers at TIR, not via AST rewriting. The doc records TIR lowerings, not AST desugarings — the title and framing should reflect this. (2) The inWild example shows Rust text output, which violates R7; entries must be TIR-level. (3) Without a CI check, Option A degrades to B within one development cycle — all Jet spec artifacts (I4 ui snapshots, I5 golden tests) are machine-enforced. (4) Option C (machine-verifiable lowering tests, a tests/lowering/ suite) should be evaluated and potentially combined with A. (5) Option D needs an explicit trigger condition ("E6 sema feature-set freeze") rather than a vague epoch reference.

options.name: docs/spec/desugaring.md + tests/lowering/ CI suite (recommended)
options.detail: Create docs/spec/desugaring.md recording each surface construct and the TIR node(s) it lowers to — at TIR level, not Rust output, so the doc survives an R7 backend swap. Simultaneously add tests/lowering/ where each surface construct has a canonical TIR expectation test. CI fails if a new surface form lacks a lowering test — matching how I4 (ui snapshots) and I5 (golden examples) work. The doc is human-readable index; the test suite is enforcement. Add "desugaring.md + lowering test updated" to the CLAUDE.md workflow done criteria.

options.name: Inline lowering notes in architecture.md (no new file)
options.detail: Add a "surface-to-TIR lowering" section to the existing architecture.md. Single-source-of-truth benefit: no contributor has to know a separate file exists. Drawback: architecture.md grows and lacks CI enforcement unless a lowering test suite is added anyway. If a lowering test suite is added, Option A and B are equivalent; prefer A because the standalone doc is more discoverable and easier to scope-limit in a grep.

options.name: Skip or defer to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not create a lowering map now. Revisit when the sema feature set is frozen for v1 API stability. Risk: the surface exceeds 40 constructs by then; contributors in E2–E5 work without the map; I8 violations (two paths to the same TIR node) are invisible until caught by a late reviewer.
options.code:
// Status quo: grep four files to find the lowering.
// grep for_in crates/jet-sema/src  -- 6 files, no canonical answer

comparisons.note: Rust Reference + MIR make many surface-to-core lowerings explicit, giving implementers and tool authors shared truth.
The Kotlin spec maintains explicit desugaring rules for lambdas, for-loops, destructuring, and delegates. It is the authoritative reference for contributors and tooling authors.
GHC's 'desugaring' phase is formally documented in the Commentary wiki. Designers check it when evaluating new syntax for overlap with existing mechanisms.
comparisons.code:
-- GHC desugars do-notation:
-- do { x <- m; rest } => m >>= \x -> rest

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust Reference + MIR make many surface-to-core lowerings explicit, giving implementers and tool authors shared truth.
decisions.recommendation: Lowering map doc + CI-enforced tests/lowering/ suite (Option A). The doc alone would rot; machine enforcement keeps it current at zero marginal cost per new feature.

decisions.title: Should Jet ship library types for TTL-bounded cache entries and expiring secrets, or defer to tracked-uncertainty work?
decisions.gist: Jet has no first-class TTL or secret-expiry types today. This decision bundles two distinct problems — cache freshness (performance/correctness) and secret memory hygiene (I1 security) — into one ballot. The cache problem is harder and carries an I8 lock-in risk; the secret-expiry problem is a clear I1 gap that can be addressed now with a well-scoped library type. The ballot should either split these or address both with sufficient design precision (closure-based ExpiringSecret access, ratified Duration constructors, a Clock.system() decision, and a cache design broad enough to be Jet's sole cache abstraction) before ratification.
decisions.explainer: A TtlCache<K,V> and an ExpiringSecret<T> are pure library types — they wrap a value with a deadline derived from the injectable Clock (already exists) and return an error or zeroize on access past expiry. No language change is required. The alternative (a type-system-level 'expires' dimension that makes staleness a compile-time property) would require tracked effects and is on the roadmap as a larger research item. Coupling these two concerns delays the useful library types for a feature that may be years away. I1: ExpiringSecret should zeroize memory on drop and on expiry by default — the safe path is automatic. I8: if we ship TtlCache now, no second cache type later.
decisions.story: I cache a JWT public key. It has a 1-hour validity. Right now nothing stops me from using a cached key past its expiry — I have to remember to check the timestamp myself. An ExpiringSecret type would refuse access after the deadline and force me to handle the 'stale' case.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) All code examples use Duration.hours(1) which is not in the ratified API (D-DET-CAPAPI ratified time.ms(n)/time.secs(n) only). Examples must be corrected before the owner can evaluate concrete syntax. (2) Clock.system() assumed in production use is not a defined constructor; ambient wall-time through Clock requires a new decision or ExpiringSecret redesign. (3) ExpiringSecret.get() returning Ok(T) produces an unzeroized clone; closure-based access (secret.with(|k| ...)) is the correct safe pattern. (4) TtlCache must either be scoped as a general eviction-policy abstraction or balloted separately — the I8 lock-in is premature. (5) D-RANDSPLIT1 (ratified) established structural isolation between security and non-security randomness; ExpiringSecret placement in core.security should reference that precedent.

options.name: Ship `ExpiringSecret<T>` now (closure access + zeroize); ballot `TtlCache` separately (recommended)
options.detail: Ship core.security.ExpiringSecret<T> with closure-based access: secret.with(|k| use_key(k)) — the closure receives a borrow, never a clone, so no unzeroized copy escapes. Zeroizes internal storage on drop and on expiry (I1). Takes a Clock parameter (from core.time.clock(seed)) for deterministic testing; resolution of Clock.system() ambient constructor is a follow-on gate before shipping. All examples must use ratified Duration constructors (time.minutes(n), time.secs(n) — not Duration.hours(n) which is unratified). TtlCache is balloted separately to get the eviction-policy design right (at minimum: capacity bounds + access-ordered eviction alongside TTL) before committing as Jet's sole cache abstraction (I8).

options.name: Defer both types to Epoch 6
options.detail: Ship neither ExpiringSecret nor TtlCache now. Developers track TTL manually with timestamps; secret zeroization is their responsibility. Sets a concrete revisit point at Epoch 6 alongside freshness/tracked-uncertainty research. Real I1 gap: secrets that should be zeroized won't be until then.

options.name: Skip both — defer to language-level freshness tracking
options.detail: Treat expiry as a type-level effect (freshness dimension) so the compiler statically flags use of a stale value. More powerful but requires tracked-effects work not yet designed. Ships nothing useful now; leaves the I1 security gap open indefinitely.

comparisons.note: Crates like `moka` and `secrecy` cover TTL caches and secret zeroization separately; no mainstream std combines both.
The secrecy crate wraps sensitive values in Secret<T> which zeroizes on drop. No TTL — expiry is still manual. Jet can do both in one type.
TTL caches are community packages in Go. No standard ExpiringSecret type. Secret zeroization requires explicit memset via unsafe. Jet can offer both safely and standardly.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust ecosystem: Crates like `moka` and `secrecy` cover TTL caches and secret zeroization separately; no mainstream std combines both.
decisions.recommendation: Ship ExpiringSecret<T> now with closure-based access and zeroize-on-drop (Option A). Ballot TtlCache separately to avoid premature I8 lock-in on cache eviction design. Fix all examples to use ratified Duration constructors before shipping.
