$ jet services enable --system   # "requires the jetpack agent; sudo to install"
^ the constraint that was never written down

comparisons.note: Daemon + root default; single-user mode exists but is second-class. Corp-laptop DOA case is common.
comparisons.code: $ sh <(curl -L https://nixos.org/nix/install) --daemon   # wants root, /nix, launchd/systemd units

comparisons.note: The model: one user-owned binary, no daemon, no root, corp-safe. Adoption followed.
The cautionary tale: root daemon became its biggest security and ops liability; rootless mode retrofitted a decade later.
comparisons.code: $ sudo systemctl start docker   # and docker group ≈ root

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U29 — Offline guarantee: once realized, envs work with zero network, forever
decisions.gist: Decide whether "realized once → works offline forever" is a tested product guarantee with an --offline enforcement flag, a best-effort behavior, or an explicit prefetch verb.
decisions.explainer: Lock + hangar already imply this: everything an env needs is content-addressed on disk after first realization. The ballot is whether jetpack promises it. The guarantee: any verb that succeeded against the current lock succeeds again with the network cable cut — jet env, jet dev, jet build, jet run, service startup, all of it. --offline makes the promise enforceable: any operation that would touch the network fails loudly with what it wanted and why, instead of hanging or silently fetching. Guarded by a golden test that realizes an env, severs network, and re-runs the full verb set. What it forbids, permanently: phone-home version checks, lazy metadata refreshes on realize verbs, telemetry in the realize path — the quiet network habits that make tools flaky on planes and in air-gapped CI.
decisions.story: Frank demos on conference wifi that died an hour ago. His repo's lock hasn't changed since yesterday; jet dev brings up postgres and the app from the hangar without noticing the network is gone. The person next to him watches npm install spin on a registry it can't reach.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev            # wifi dead, lock unchanged since yesterday
✓ env.dev realized from hangar (0.1s) · ✓ postgres healthy · app on :8080
# no timeout, no retry spinner — network was never consulted

$ jet update codex --offline
Error [E1258]: `jet update` needs the network (queries github@openai/codex releases)
 Why: --offline forbids all network access
 Fix: drop --offline, or pin the wanted rev explicitly

# air-gapped CI:
$ jet build --offline   # cache miss = loud failure naming the object, never a fetch
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 6). Semantics: verbs classify as realize-class (env/dev/run/build/test/services — never touch network when lock is satisfied; with --offline, hard-fail instead of fetch on any miss) or network-class (update/outdated/add/publish/cache push — honestly network-bound, refuse under --offline with E1258 naming the need). Channel refs (U21) resolve only in network-class verbs, so they cannot break the guarantee. Interlocks: U22 auto-GC must never collect objects the current locks reference (already its retention floor) or GC could break the promise; U24 substitution is an optimization inside realize-class verbs — a cache miss falls back to local build, and under --offline to a loud failure. Golden test shape: realize → deny network at the process level → full verb sweep must pass.

options.name: Hard guarantee + --offline enforcement + golden test (recommended)
options.detail: Realized-once-works-forever is product contract: realize-class verbs never consult the network when the lock is satisfied; --offline turns any would-be fetch into a loud E1258; golden test enforces it in CI permanently.
options.code:
$ jet env --offline      # lock satisfied → identical to jet env
$ jet env --offline      # after a lock bump with an unfetched object:
Error [E1258]: `codex` v0.50.1 is not in the hangar and --offline forbids fetching
 Fix: run `jet env` once with network, or push the object to a reachable cache

options.name: Best-effort offline, no promise, no flag
options.detail: Architecture already mostly delivers it; ship without the contract or the test. Costs nothing today — and erodes silently the first time a feature adds a metadata ping to jet env, which nothing would catch.
options.code:
$ jet dev    # on a plane, some future version:
checking for updates… (30s timeout)   ← the ping nobody balloted

options.name: Explicit prefetch verb required (jet fetch)
options.detail: Offline use is opt-in preparation: jet fetch downloads everything the lock needs; realize verbs may otherwise fetch lazily. Honest, but makes offline a mode users must anticipate — Frank's demo dies because he didn't run the magic verb yesterday.
options.code:
$ jet fetch              # yesterday, with wifi — did you remember?
$ jet dev                # today, offline: works only if you did

comparisons.note: Mostly offline-capable in practice, never promised; eval can still surprise-fetch (flake inputs, tarballs), and failures hang on timeouts instead of failing fast.
comparisons.code: $ nix develop   # on a plane: …waiting on github.com…

comparisons.note: The precedent: --offline exists, fails loudly with the missing crate named, and vendoring is a supported workflow. Users trust it.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build --offline
error: no matching package named `foo` found (offline mode)

comparisons.note: The anti-model: --offline exists but registry metadata habits make it unreliable; nobody trusts it, so nobody uses it.
comparisons.code: $ npm ci --offline   # works, sometimes, depending on cache weather

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: Contextual dot-member blocks inside marker scopes: how does a #Test block spell its vocabulary?
decisions.gist: Inside a block marker like #Test, should typing `.` offer scope-specific sub-blocks (`.expect_fail { … }`), and what is the one general rule for all scoped markers?
decisions.explainer: A block marker (#Test("name") { … }, #Bench, #Transact) creates a scope with its own vocabulary: a test can expect failure, run setup, set a timeout, skip on a condition. Today that vocabulary has no home — S82 gives markers arguments and bodies, but no way for a scope to offer named sub-blocks over a region of its body. This decision picks the spelling for scope vocabulary: the thing the editor suggests when you type inside a marker block, and the thing a reader sees marking a region. Whatever wins becomes the ONE spelling (I8) for every scoped marker, not a #Test special case.
decisions.story: Betty is writing parser tests. One case documents a known bug — the parser wrongly accepts an empty config file — and she wants just that region of the test marked expected-to-fail until the bug is fixed, without splitting the file into a second test or memorizing a new top-level marker. She types `.` on a fresh line inside the #Test block and wants the editor to show her exactly what a test scope can do.
decisions.detail: Interplay: the two-plane law (D-MARKER-FAMILY1) is untouched — scope members are per-scope vocabulary, not new global markers; S82 grammar shapes stay. If B is ratified, other block markers (#Bench, #Transact, #Unsafe) may later declare members under the same law, each addition being an API decision, not a syntax one. Whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test before shipping, and the unknown-member diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4). Recommendation rationale: B is the only option that gives region granularity AND a closed, teachable vocabulary with a great error, and it is the strongest LSP-discoverability move — rank on beginner experience and one-path.

options.name: Marker arguments only — no new syntax
options.detail: Whole-block flags via existing marker arguments. Region granularity means splitting into more tests. Zero new grammar; vocabulary lives in the marker's signature and LSP completes argument labels. The cost: Betty's one-region case forces a file reorganization, and scope words that wrap code (setup, expected-fail region) have no honest spelling.

options.name: Contextual dot-member blocks (recommended)
options.detail: General law: inside a #Marker { } block body, a statement-position `.name { … }` or `.name(args) { … }` resolves against that marker's declared scope members. Unknown member is a teaching error that lists the scope's whole vocabulary. Typing `.` in statement position inside the block pops the member menu — the Blueprint-style 'what can I do here' move. Per I8 this becomes the ONLY spelling for scope vocabulary (no parallel nested-marker spelling for the same job). Grammar is unambiguous: distinguished from a leading-dot enum value (`.Circle(2.0)`, D-ENUMDOT1) by the required trailing `{ … }` block; from dot-construction `.{` and inferred destructuring (S74) by the identifier after the dot; method calls need a receiver expression.

options.name: Nested scoped markers
options.detail: Reuse S82's existing `#Marker { }` statement grammar: #ExpectFail("bug #412") { … } is legal only inside #Test. Vocabulary = which markers are legal in which scopes; discoverability = marker completion filtered by context. No new grammar, but the global # plane grows a per-scope directive for every scope word, and the page reads heavier — a reader must know #ExpectFail is test-only, not a general directive.

options.name: Block-valued marker arguments
options.detail: Scope vocabulary stays in the marker head; arguments may take blocks. Everything is one mechanism (marker args), but the head gets heavy for real tests, ordering between the main body and argument blocks is invisible (does setup run before the body? where does the reader look?), and a region in the middle of a test can't be expressed at all.

comparisons.note: Implicit member expressions: `.red` resolves against the expected type. Same discoverability move, expression position only.
DSL receivers: test frameworks offer scope words as lambdas-with-receiver; powerful but any function can be a 'scope word' — no closed vocabulary, weak errors.
#[should_panic] is whole-function only; no region granularity, discovered by memorization.
test.failing — whole test, dot-discoverable off the test object.

decisions.title: U30 — Toolchain as a dependency: does pkg.jet pin the jet version, with any jet auto-fetching and re-executing it?
decisions.gist: Should a project's pkg.jet name which jet version builds it, so any installed jet automatically fetches that toolchain and delegates to it — making clone-and-run just work forever?
decisions.explainer: Today the jet that builds a project is whatever is on PATH. A project written on jet 0.4 may use spellings jet 0.6 removed (or not yet have spellings it needs), so an old project greets a new machine with a wall of errors that look like the project is broken. The proposal treats the toolchain itself as a dependency: pkg.jet names a jet version; any jet binary reading the manifest realizes that toolchain into the hangar like any other package and re-executes itself as that version (the same exec dispatch already ratified in D-JPK-DISPATCH1). One law makes this safe forever: the pkg.jet identity block (the payload: block and jet: line) stays parseable by every future jet — frozen-forward grammar — so an old jet can always read enough of a newer project to fetch the right toolchain.
decisions.story: Hank clones a teammate's simulation repo six months after it was written. His laptop has jet 0.6; the project was built on 0.4 and uses a spelling 0.6 removed. Without a pin, `jet run` prints forty syntax errors and Hank concludes the project is rotten. With the pin, it prints `project pins jet 0.4 — fetching 0.4.2 (12 MB)… done` and runs.
decisions.detail: Bootstrap law (ships with A): the pkg.jet identity block — the `payload:` block and `jet:` line — has frozen-forward grammar; every future jet parses at least that block of every past and future manifest, so version dispatch can never be wedged by manifest evolution (Go proved this contract works at ecosystem scale). Version-proliferation is bounded by hangar GC (D-JPK-GC1) and shared caches (D-JPK-CACHE1). Interplay with the minimal-surface rule (U7/U10): no new files, no new commands — one field in the one reserved manifest, verbs on the one command. Recommendation rationale: A is the only option where the beginner's first contact with an old project succeeds; rank on beginner experience and long-term correctness.

options.name: Pin + auto-realize + exec (recommended)
options.detail: pkg.jet gets a `jet:` field (channel semantics per D-JPK-CHANNEL1; the lock records the exact version). A jet whose version differs from the pin realizes the pinned toolchain into the hangar — prebuilt objects via the D-JPK-CACHE1 substitution path, offline thereafter per D-JPK-OFFLINE1, GC'd per D-JPK-GC1, no Nix required per D-JPK-NONIX1, no daemon/root per D-JPK-NODAEMON1 — and execs it (D-JPK-DISPATCH1 mechanism). Frozen-forward identity-block law ships with it. `jet toolchain` shows the pin; `jet update jet` moves it deliberately.
options.code:
// pkg.jet
payload: { name: "sim_dashboard", version: "0.3.0" }
jet: 0.4

$ jet run .
jet: project pins toolchain 0.4 (installed: 0.6.1)
jet: realizing jet 0.4.2 into hangar… done
building sim_dashboard… ok

$ jet toolchain
pinned: 0.4 (locked 0.4.2, hangar) — installed: 0.6.1

$ jet update jet
jet: 0.4 -> 0.6 updates 3 spellings; run `jet fix` after. Proceed? [y/N]

options.name: Warn only (engines-style)
options.detail: Mismatch prints a warning naming the pinned version, then proceeds with the installed jet. No fetch machinery, but the warning scrolls past and Hank still gets the forty errors — Node's engines shows exactly how this decays into a convention nobody trusts.
options.code:
$ jet run .
warning: project pins jet 0.4, installed is 0.6.1 — output may not build
error[E0xxx]: unknown spelling `…` (x40)

options.name: Dev-shell only — toolchain is an env.jet package
options.detail: The toolchain pins only inside the dev shell: env.jet lists jet@0.4 in packages; `jet dev` / `jetpack enter` use it; a bare `jet run` outside the shell uses whatever is installed. Consistent with 'env.jet is dev shell only', but the beginner path — clone, `jet run` — is exactly the path left unprotected.

options.name: No pin — editions carry compatibility
options.detail: pkg.jet declares `edition: 2027`; one jet binary keeps every edition's grammar alive, so new compilers always build old code. This is the Rust editions bet — but editions cover surface grammar, not stdlib behavior, codegen differences, or pre-1.0 breakage, and they obligate the compiler to carry every historical grammar forever. Editions remain a good complementary idea after 1.0; they are not a substitute for a pin while the language moves fast.

comparisons.note: The gold standard: go.mod's toolchain directive; any Go ≥1.21 auto-downloads and re-executes the pinned toolchain. Clone-and-run just works.
rust-toolchain.toml; works, but only because a separate manager (rustup) intercepts every invocation — a resident middleman jetpack's no-daemon law avoids.
engines is warn-only and widely ignored; teams bolt on nvm/.nvmrc by convention. The cautionary tale for option B.
Flake pin: exact and hermetic, but the pin lives outside the language's own manifest and costs the whole Nix mental model.

decisions.title: Next-generation FFI: what one structure makes every foreign language near-trivial to wrap, replace in situ, and tap immediately?
decisions.gist: Pick the architecture every foreign language shares: per-language namespaces with pluggable binders, uniform extern blocks, typed projection importers, or runtime-broker sidecars.
decisions.explainer: Jet already speaks two foreign languages, each with its own shape: Rust via extern rust "crate@version" { … } (S50) and C via generated bindings mounted at c.<lib> with a user overlay (S59). JS is sequenced next, Swift later (D-JSWIFTFFI1). The owner's bar: using a library from almost any language should feel almost as easy as using a Jet package — every ecosystem's work immediately usable, and any foreign dependency replaceable later by a native Jet implementation without touching call sites (in-situ replacement). This ballot picks the one structure all languages share. How deep each language's binding goes (shallow declaration binding, full typed projection, or a runtime broker) is a per-language follow-up ballot on top of the winning frame — the frame is what must never vary.
decisions.story: Doris is building a lab-data tool in Jet. The only mature reader for her instrument's file format is a Python package; the best plotting library is on npm; a checksum routine she needs ships as a C header. She wants all three working this afternoon, each behind an ordinary typed Jet API with honest effects — and when a native Jet plotting package appears next year, she wants to swap it in by changing one dependency line, not rewriting call sites.
decisions.inWild:
use py.h5instrument as h5     // Python package, typed surface
use js.plotly as plot          // npm package (D-NPMTYPE1 stubs)
use "xxhash.h" as xx           // C header, script tier (S59)

fn main() #(Fs, Proc) {
    run := h5.read("run-0142.h5")
    print(xx.hash64(run.raw))
    plot.line(run.times, run.values)
}
decisions.detail: A, C, and D compose rather than exclude: A is the surface law (namespaces, three tiers, overlay, in-situ shadowing, lockfile provenance); C and D are per-language binder strategies BEHIND that surface — projection importers for static languages (C, Swift, Rust), a broker likely right for Python/JS dynamic tails, shallow declaration binding where that's enough. Ratifying A means: the surface ships now; follow-up ballots (D-FFI-PY1, D-FFI-JS1 folding in D-NPMTYPE1, D-FFI-SWIFT1 honoring D-JSWIFTFFI1 sequencing) pick each language's strategy on the common frame. Existing ratifications are preserved, not reopened: S59 is already the C instance of A; S50's extern rust block becomes the rust binder's declaration format inside rust.*; D-DEP1's vendoring/hash-pinning law extends to every language's refs. I8: one FFI structure for all languages is the point — shipping B alongside A would be two spellings for one job. I1/I2 hold in every option: user code is safe unless #Unsafe; no foreign toolchain's errors ever reach the user unlaundered — binder diagnostics are Jet diagnostics with codes and snapshots (I4). Recommendation rationale: A is the only option that is uniform (one structure to learn), immediate (a new language needs only a binder, at whatever depth exists first), deep where it counts (projection strategy per language later), and structurally in-situ-replaceable — rank on beginner experience, one-path, and long-term correctness.

options.name: Language namespaces + pluggable binders (recommended)
options.detail: Generalize S59's proven C structure into the law for every language. Each foreign world mounts as a namespace <lang>.<lib> with the same three tiers everywhere: script tier (use "xxhash.h" as xx — bind on first compile), project tier (use py.h5instrument as h5 with the dep pinned in pkg.jet), overlay tier (#Extern module py.h5instrument { … } to refine generated types; overlay wins). `jet bind <lang>` is a per-language binder producing inspectable, committable bindings in .jet/bindings/<lang>/<lib>.jet. Safety: generated bindings are safe wrappers by construction (marshaling internals compiler-vetted like std internals — I1); calling a foreign symbol outside a binding requires #Unsafe("reason"). In-situ replacement is structural: any <lang>.<lib> can be shadowed by a Jet package exporting the same surface — call sites never change. Per-language depth (projection vs broker vs shallow) is chosen behind this surface, one follow-up ballot per language.

options.name: Uniform extern blocks (generalize S50)
options.detail: Every language uses S50's declaration-first shape: extern <lang> "ref@version" { fn … = "path" }. Maximal explicitness — every crossing is written in the file — and one grammar for all languages. The cost is the wall: wrapping a real library means hundreds of declaration lines per library (generated or not, they live in your project), there is no namespace to shadow so in-situ replacement means hand-built wrapper modules, and 'almost trivial' is exactly what it isn't.

options.name: Typed projection importers only
options.detail: Every language gets a full compiler importer (Swift-Clang-importer style): use py.h5instrument elaborates the package's surface — from type stubs and introspection — directly into checked Jet types with effects and ownership mapped; overlays refine (raw pointer -> checked handle). The deepest 'feels native' ceiling, and the right end-state for static languages. As the only mechanism, it makes every new language wait for a full importer before ANY access exists — the opposite of tapping ecosystems immediately.

options.name: Runtime broker sidecars only
options.detail: Foreign runtimes run as supervised sidecar processes with a typed message boundary; py.* calls marshal to a Python worker (Mojo's play). Any language with a runtime works day one and effects are honest (#(Proc) on every call) — but values are serialized at every crossing (no zero-copy, no shared memory), C headers and Rust crates don't fit the model at all, and production binaries grow a process tree. Right as a per-language strategy for dynamic tails; wrong as the only structure.

comparisons.note: @cImport makes C trivial — but only C. The lesson: binder-in-the-compiler is magic; the miss: no structure for a second language.
Clang importer: full typed projection of C/ObjC — foreign APIs feel native. The depth ceiling to aim per-language binders at.
comparisons.code: import Accelerate   // C library, arrives as typed Swift

comparisons.note: Imports any Python module day one via a runtime broker — instant ecosystem reach, marshaled boundary. The play for dynamic-language tails.
comparisons.code:
from python import Python
let np = Python.import_module("numpy")

comparisons.note: P/Invoke plus WinRT projections: two tiers under one runtime — proof that shallow decls and deep projections coexist behind one surface.
Polyglot: many languages, one VM — reach bought with total runtime lock-in; the anti-goal for an AOT language.

decisions.title: Nested variant groups in `enum`: can a variant hold sub-variants so a group name matches its whole subtree?
decisions.gist: Can enum variants nest into groups, so testing `.Fire` also matches `.Fire.Burn` and `.Fire.Scald`?
decisions.explainer: Cross-system code constantly needs a name-tree: damage kinds, permission scopes, diagnostic categories, feature flags. UE ships this as stringly GameplayTags (Damage.Fire.Burn) matched by ancestry, which composes beautifully but renames break silently and there is no counting (two stuns applied, one removed, still stunned). Jet already has closed enums, leading-dot values (D-ENUMDOT1), and the ==-pattern law (S31). This decision adds one axis to `enum`: a variant may group sub-variants, and a group name matches its subtree in == and match arms. No new keyword — the `tag` spelling was killed for colliding with the ratified D-QUAL2 tag qualifier and minting a second closed-name mechanism beside enum (I8). Also on the table: a core `Bag<T>` counted multiset (sibling of Set) so `add`/`remove` counts correctly, and whether `Bag.has(.Fire)` accepts a subtree pattern as sugar for the `any` closure.
decisions.story: Hank is building the damage system for a roguelike. He has two physical damage kinds, two fire kinds, and cold, and armor should soak any physical hit. Today he lists every physical leaf by hand in the armor check; the day he adds a pierce variant he forgets to update it and armor silently stops working against it. He also tracks active damage-over-time in a Set, so a second fire tick and one cure leaves the target un-burning when it should still burn.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: it is the one path that makes the tree a compile-time fact (exhaustiveness, rename-safe, LSP-completable) using machinery beginners already know, with counting handled by a plain core container; the `has` sugar (D) can follow as a library call once A ships. · This ballot was minted from tools/Tower/docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Nested variant groups, leaf-only payloads (recommended)
options.detail: A variant may enclose sub-variants in `{ }`; a group name matches its whole subtree in == and match arms; exhaustiveness is checked at the group level; payloads live on leaves only. Ships alongside a core `Bag<T>` counted multiset so add/remove counts correctly. `Bag.has` stays an explicit `any` closure for subtree queries. Renames become refactors, the LSP completes every `.` level, and a value is always a leaf.

options.name: Enum-of-enums (Rust-style nesting, no new syntax)
options.detail: No grammar change: model the tree as separate enums carried as payloads. Ancestor tests become `d is .Physical(_)`; you carry a second type name per group and there is no subtree-level exhaustiveness or dot-path value. Cheapest surface, but the group name is not a value and the compiler cannot see the tree.

options.name: Flat enum + naming convention (status quo, reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Keep `PhysicalBlunt`, `FireBurn` and match ancestry by hand with an else arm. Honest baseline: no new mechanism, but every subtree check is hand-maintained and silently rots when a leaf is added, and there is no counted container so multiset bugs stay.

options.name: Grouping plus subtree-pattern sugar on `Bag.has` (A, extended)
options.detail: Everything in A, and additionally `Bag.has(.Fire)` accepts a subtree pattern as sugar for the `any` closure, so counted-multiset ancestor queries read as one call. More reach, one more thing to learn on the container; the sugar must be exactly equivalent to the closure to avoid a second meaning (I8).
options.code:
active.add(.Fire.Burn)
active.has(.Fire)        // sugar for active.any((t) => t == .Fire)  -> true
active.has(.Fire.Scald) // false

comparisons.note: Swift nests enums inside enums; ancestor matching is by hand (`if case .physical = d`), no subtree exhaustiveness.
GameplayTags are stringly dot-paths matched by ancestry (`.HasTag("Damage.Fire")` catches `Damage.Fire.Burn`). Renames break silently; no compile check.
No grouping axis; nest enum-in-enum and match with a wildcard arm. No subtree name, no counting container in std.
comparisons.code:
enum Damage { Physical(Physical), Fire(Fire), Cold }
match d { Damage::Physical(_) => armor(), _ => {} }

comparisons.note: Discriminated unions with a shared prefix or a nested `kind` field; ancestry is a manual string `startsWith` or a switch group.

decisions.title: `@[Patchable]` derive: generate a typed `T.Patch` change-value you can hold, diff, merge and serialize?
decisions.gist: Should a derive generate a typed `T.Patch` — an all-optional twin of a struct — that you can hold, apply later, diff, merge and log?
decisions.explainer: Jet's ratified `.{ }` copy-update (D-COPYUPDATE1) applies a change now. But a change you hold for later — an undo stack, an audit log, an API PATCH body, optimistic-UI predict-then-reconcile — is hand-rolled per type today: an optional-field struct plus a merge function, written again for every record. UE's insight (GameplayEffect) is that a change should be a data value: previewable, loggable, revertible, sendable. This decision picks a derive on the `@` contract plane (like `@Codable`) that generates a nested `T.Patch` struct whose fields are all optional, plus `apply`/`diff`/`merge`, Codable by construction. No new expression syntax — you build a Patch with ordinary `.{ }`. Killed already: relative magnitudes (`level: +1`), which are literal semantics found nowhere else; `invert(base)`, a footgun valid only against its exact base; duration/stacking policy, which is library speculation.
decisions.story: Doris maintains the employee directory for a mid-size firm. It has an undo button and an audit log. For every kind of record she writes an optional-field struct and a merge function by hand, once per type, forever; and the audit log stores freeform JSON that slowly drifts out of sync with the real field names. She wants one canonical 'here is the change' value she can apply, reverse, and log without writing the plumbing again.
decisions.inWild:
@[Patchable]
struct Employee {
    level: Int
    title: String
    team: String
}

promote :: Employee.Patch.{ level: 4, title: "Senior" }   // ordinary .{ } — set fields = the change
emp2    :: emp.apply(promote)
undo    :: Employee.diff(emp2, emp)      // the patch that gets you back
both    :: promote.merge(relocate)       // right side wins on overlap
audit.log(promote)                       // Patch is Codable by construction
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: one canonical, typed, serializable change value (I8) that reuses `.{ }`, pattern-matching and Codable, and kills the hand-rolled-patch bug class outright; the full apply/diff/merge surface is what the driving use cases (undo, audit, optimistic UI, DB partials) actually require. · This ballot was minted from tools/Tower/docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: `@[Patchable]` derive → `T.Patch` struct + apply/diff/merge, Codable (recommended)
options.detail: A derive on the `@` plane generates a nested all-optional `T.Patch` struct plus `apply(base)`, `Type.diff(new, old)`, and `merge(other)`; the Patch is Codable by construction. You construct and read it with skills you already have (`.{ }`, field access, patterns). `apply` is defined in terms of `.{ }` semantics, so there is one meaning of "edited copy" (I8 seam: `.{ }` is change-applied-now, Patch is change-as-a-value).

options.name: Generic library `Patch<T>` type (no per-struct codegen)
options.detail: A single std generic instead of a derive: one type for all structs, no generated code. But field access becomes dynamic/stringly — you lose field-name completion, compile-checked field names, and exhaustiveness. The value is opaque to the type system, which is exactly what a typed patch was meant to fix.
options.code:
p: Patch<Employee> := Patch.new()
p.set("title", "Staff")         // field name is a string; typo compiles
emp2 :: p.apply(emp)

options.name: Manual optional-field structs (status quo, reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Keep hand-writing an optional-field struct and an apply/merge function per record type. No new mechanism, but the plumbing, the diff code, and the audit-log drift all stay, re-implemented everywhere.

options.name: `@[Patchable]` derive, apply-only (defer diff/merge)
options.detail: Generate `T.Patch` and `apply` only; leave `diff` and `merge` to a later library decision. Smallest surface that still gives one canonical change value and Codable serialization. The cost: undo (diff) and combining changes (merge) — two of the four driving use cases — have no answer yet.

comparisons.note: TypeScript `Partial<T>` gives the all-optional twin type for free, and JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) standardizes apply. But there is no diff, no field-wise merge helper, and null-vs-absent is ambiguous.
comparisons.code:
type EmployeePatch = Partial<Employee>;
const next = { ...emp, ...promote };   // apply; no diff, no typed merge

comparisons.note: No built-in. A derive crate or a hand-written struct of `Option<T>` fields plus an apply fn; diff/merge are bespoke each time.
comparisons.code:
struct EmployeePatch { level: Option<i32>, title: Option<String> }
fn apply(e: Employee, p: EmployeePatch) -> Employee { /* per-field ?? */ }

comparisons.note: No built-in partial type. Teams hand-roll an optional-field struct or use key-path writes; no standard diff or merge.
comparisons.code: struct EmployeePatch { var level: Int?; var title: String? }

comparisons.note: A GameplayEffect is data: a modifier list applied to attributes, previewable and reversible — but game-specific, not a general record patch.

decisions.title: Computed struct fields: can a field be a formula over its siblings — `attack: Int => strength*2+gear_mod`?
decisions.gist: Can a struct field be defined by a formula over its sibling fields, recomputed on every read instead of stored?
decisions.explainer: UE's attribute sets bake clamping and derivation into the field so no caller can produce a -3 health. Jet already has the clamping half: `type Health :: Int(0..1000)` (D-RANGETYPE1) and `#Invariant` (D-REFINE1). The missing half is a field defined by its siblings. Today that is a zero-arg method — which works, but is invisible to `@Codable` output and, the moment someone stores the value for speed or serialization, goes stale. This decision adds a computed field: `name: T => expr` where the expression reads sibling fields. It recomputes under `.{ }` and patches, appears in Codable encode, is unsettable (assigning it is an error with a fix-it), and takes no parens. The spelling uses `=>` (already 'computes to', from lambdas); `=` is left free for the eventual field-default decision, which every mainstream language spells with `=`. Cycles are a compile error; derived-from-derived is allowed, dependency-ordered.
decisions.story: Earl is writing the character sheet for a tabletop companion app. Attack power is strength times two plus gear bonus. He stores attack as a plain Int field and computes it in the constructor. A week later a teammate edits strength through a copy-update on the saved character; attack keeps its old value, the sheet shows the wrong number, and the bug hides because everything type-checks.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: the standard cross-language spelling for derived state, it kills the stale-denormalized-field bug class at the source, composes with patches (base/current for free), and keeps one authoring story per job by staying the non-reactive twin of `Computed<T>`. · This ballot was minted from tools/Tower/docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Computed field `name: T => expr` (recommended)
options.detail: A field whose value is an expression over sibling fields, evaluated on read. Recomputes under `.{ }` and patches, appears in `@Codable` encode, is unsettable (assignment is a teaching error with a fix-it), takes no parens. `=>` already means 'computes to'; `=` stays reserved for the future field-default slot. Cycles are a compile error; derived-from-derived is allowed, dependency-ordered.

options.name: Keep zero-arg methods (status quo, honest reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Derived values stay methods. Semantically the same result, but the value is absent from `@Codable` output, does not recompute inside a copy-update automatically (the method is fine but a stored cache is not), and reads as `s.attack()` with parens. No new spelling — and the stale-cache bug class stays whenever anyone denormalizes for speed or serialization.

options.name: Computed field, excluded from Codable output
options.detail: Same `name: T => expr` spelling and recompute-in-copy behavior, but treated as transient: never encoded, always recomputed on decode. Simpler contract (no encode ambiguity), but loses the base/current-in-the-wire-format win — a client that only has the JSON cannot read the derived value without the schema.

options.name: `#[Computed]` marker on a method (no new field grammar)
options.detail: Reuse method syntax with a marker that opts the method into Codable output and parens-free access, instead of a new field form. Avoids adding grammar to the struct body, but still reads as a method declaration and introduces a marker to learn; the `=>` field form is the more direct spelling of "this field is derived".

comparisons.note: Swift computed properties are the standard spelling: a stored-free property with a getter body, no parens at the call site.
A `val` with a custom getter — same idea, computed on read, no backing field.
comparisons.code: val attack: Int get() = strength * 2 + gearMod

comparisons.note: Expression-bodied property; recomputes on every access.
No computed fields; you write a method and call `s.attack()`. It is invisible to serde `derive(Serialize)` unless you add attributes by hand.
comparisons.code: impl Stats { fn attack(&self) -> i32 { self.strength * 2 + self.gear_mod } }

decisions.title: Reopen D-EFF4/5: make the effect vocabulary a tree with ancestor subsumption (`#(Fs.Read)` under `#(Fs)`)?
decisions.gist: Reopen the flat effect list: let effects nest so `#(Fs)` accepts any `Fs.*`, and `#(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` callee?
decisions.explainer: D-EFF4/5 deliberately ratified a flat, closed set of ten effects — Net, Fs, Io, Db, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, Log, Gpu — with NO subsumption (calling a `Net` effect under `#(Io)` is E0740). It was chosen for teachability: ten names, no taxonomy arguments. This is the one gameplay-dna transplant that reopens a decided question, and it carries that burden explicitly. The proposal: re-base the ten names as tree roots so `Fs.Read`, `Fs.Write`, `Net.Http.Get` are leaves, and ancestor matching IS subsumption — the exact same rule as the tag trees in D-TAG1, learned once. `#(Fs)` in a signature would accept any `Fs.*` callee; a `#(Fs.Read)` caller would reject an `Fs.Write` callee; `#Grant` (D-SCAP1) gains subtree precision. Existing flat names stay valid as roots, so there is no migration break. It also settles the acknowledged D-EFF2 subsumption documentation gap structurally. Sequence this last, behind D-TAG1/PATCH1/FIELDPOL1.
decisions.story: Walter is hardening a backend service. He has a config loader that should only ever read the filesystem, and he wants the compiler to prove it can never delete a file. Today `#(Fs)` is one indivisible capability: read and write are the same grant, so the loader is trusted with deletes and a stray `remove()` slipped past review would type-check clean. Read/write precision on Fs, Db and Net is the refinement his team asks for most.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A on the merits: it delivers the most-requested read/write capability precision, unifies subtree matching with D-TAG1 into one rule learned once, and settles the D-EFF2 gap structurally with zero migration break — but it reopens ratified D-EFF4/5, so sequence it last behind the other three. · This ballot was minted from tools/Tower/docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Effect tree with ancestor subsumption (recommended)
options.detail: The ten ratified names become roots; `Fs.Read`, `Fs.Write`, `Net.Http.Get` are leaves. `#(Fs)` accepts any `Fs.*` callee; `#(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` callee; `#Grant` gains subtree precision. Flat names remain valid as roots, so no existing code breaks. Reverses E0740. Ancestor matching is the same rule as D-TAG1, so a user learns subtree matching once and applies it to enums, tags and effects alike.

options.name: Keep flat, no subsumption (status quo, defer)
options.detail: Do nothing. Ten names, no taxonomy, E0740 stays; the model stays maximally teachable but there is no read/write precision, and the acknowledged D-EFF2 subsumption gap stays a documentation note rather than a structural answer. Walter cannot prove his loader is read-only.
options.code:
fn load(p: String) -> Config #(Fs)   // read and write are one grant
fn read_only(p: String) #(Fs) { remove(p) }  // type-checks — no way to forbid write

options.name: Fixed two-level split on a few effects only
options.detail: Add a curated, closed second level to just the effects that need it — `Fs.Read`/`Fs.Write`, `Net.In`/`Net.Out`, `Db.Read`/`Db.Write` — with no general nesting. Less taxonomy debate than open trees, but the second level is picked arbitrarily by the language and the rule is a special case rather than the general ancestor law shared with D-TAG1.

options.name: Precision via prohibition, not a tree
options.detail: Express read-only by combining the flat name with a D-PROP1 prohibition instead of nesting: `#(Fs) #(!Fs.Write)`. Keeps the ten flat names and adds no hierarchy, but the spelling is compound, `Fs.Write` still has to be a nameable sub-capability (so you half-need the tree anyway), and it does not compose with `#Grant` subtree precision.
options.code: fn read_only(p: String) #(Fs) #(!Fs.Write) { load(p) }  // remove(p) here -> prohibition error

comparisons.note: Deno's permission model splits filesystem into --allow-read and --allow-write, and read/write accept path prefixes — hierarchical capability, granted outside the type system.
GameplayTag subsumption again: a system requiring `Ability.Fire` is satisfied by `Ability.Fire.Fireball`. Same ancestor rule proposed here for effects.
Effects are rows of labels with no hierarchy; you get precise per-effect tracking but express read-vs-write as two unrelated labels, not parent/child.
No effect system; capability is by module privacy and the type of the handle you hold (e.g. `&File` vs write methods). No signature-level effect at all.

decisions.gist: Which app is Jet's flagship CLI slice — the command-line program we ship, benchmark, and point people at.
decisions.story: Hank, a sysadmin who lives in a terminal, hears Jet is 'great for CLI tools.' He wants proof: one real tool he can build from source, run on his own files, and time against what he already uses. Whatever we ship here is that proof — it gets compared, benchmarked, and quoted.
decisions.detail: [Owner 2026-07-03: flagship slices deferred to END of Epoch 4 — jetpack development takes priority. Web-app slice candidate when resumed: recreate Tower itself in Jet (owner suggestion, recorded on card #9).]

options.name: jetgrep — recursive regex search (recommended)
options.detail: Grow the E2 GA jetgrep into a ripgrep-class searcher: globs, ignore rules, --count/--files/--context, colored TTY output, parallel directory scan. Invites the single highest-signal CLI benchmark that exists (vs grep/ripgrep) and exercises regex, fs walk, streaming stdin, args, color, exit codes.
options.code:
$ jetgrep "fn \\w+_test" src/ --count
src/lexer.jet: 14
src/parser.jet: 22

$ time jetgrep TODO ~/big-repo   # the benchmark people will actually run
real 0m0.41s

$ jetgrep "(unclosed" src/
error: invalid pattern: unclosed group
  fix: escape the parenthesis: \\(

options.name: jetstat — typed CSV/JSON data cruncher
options.detail: Reads CSV with a header row into typed rows, filters, aggregates, emits JSON. Showcases serde derives, iterator adapters, and typed-pipeline safety — the 'awk but typed' pitch. Weaker on raw-speed comparison; stronger on type-safety story.
options.code:
$ jetstat sales.csv --filter "amount > 100" --group region --out json
{"west": {"count": 1204, "total": 981223.50}, "east": ...}

$ jetstat sales.csv --filter "amont > 100"
error: no column `amont` in sales.csv
  fix: did you mean `amount`?

options.name: jetship — static site generator
options.detail: Markdown tree in, HTML site out: templates, front-matter, live rebuild via jet dev. Credible (Hugo/Zola class), touches text/fs/templating, and its output can host Jet's own docs. Benchmarks less crisply than search; templating surface is a bigger bite.
options.code:
$ jetship build site/
  42 pages -> public/ in 180ms
$ jetship dev site/
  serving http://localhost:8080  (rebuild on save)

options.name: jetwatch — parallel task runner / file watcher
options.detail: make-meets-watchexec: declares tasks in a typed manifest, runs them in parallel on file change. Shows tasks/channels and process control in a tool devs run all day. Overlaps `jet dev` conceptually — risks a second way to mean 'watch and rerun' (I8 adjacency).
options.code:
$ jetwatch test lint
[test] 132 passed  [lint] clean   (parallel, 2.1s)
[watch] src/parser.jet changed -> rerunning test

options.name: jetdu — parallel disk-usage analyzer
options.detail: ncdu-class: walks a tree in parallel, ranks by size, TUI summary table. Simple mental model, good parallel-fs and TUI-table showcase. Narrower feature spread than A-C (no regex/serde/templates).
options.code:
$ jetdu ~/Projects
  3.2G  jet/target
  1.1G  jet/.jet/store
  212M  photos/raw
scanned 148,201 files in 0.6s

decisions.comparisons: Rust's domain proof is ripgrep — one tool did more for Rust's CLI reputation than any doc. Go's is the gh/docker generation of CLIs. Zig points at its own build system. The pattern: one polished, benchmarkable tool per language.
decisions.rec: A — the grep head-to-head is the strongest single proof a language is fast and pleasant for CLI work, and the heritage jetgrep already GA'd once, so the slice measures polish, not feasibility.
decisions.recommendation: A — the grep head-to-head is the strongest single proof a language is fast and pleasant for CLI work, and the heritage jetgrep already GA'd once, so the slice measures polish, not feasibility.

decisions.gist: Which service is Jet's flagship server slice — the HTTP program that proves the backend story.
decisions.story: Doris runs a small team's internal tools on one VM. She'll adopt Jet for services the day she can read one real service — routes, database, logging, shutdown — deploy it as a single binary, and curl it. This slice is that service.
decisions.detail: [Owner 2026-07-03: flagship slices deferred to END of Epoch 4 — jetpack development takes priority. Web-app slice candidate when resumed: recreate Tower itself in Jet (owner suggestion, recorded on card #9).]

options.name: jetpaste — pastebin with TTL expiry (recommended)
options.detail: POST a paste, get a short id; GET raw or HTML; expiry via TTL sweep; /stats and /health. CRUD + persistence + time + concurrent clients is the minimum honest service, and every behavior goldens through curl. Exercises routes, SQLite, serde JSON, structured logs, per-request deadlines, graceful shutdown.
options.code:
$ jetpaste &
$ curl -d "hello world" localhost:8080/paste
{"id": "k3xq", "expires": "2026-07-03T12:00:00Z"}
$ curl localhost:8080/p/k3xq
hello world
$ curl localhost:8080/p/gone4
{"error": "not found or expired"}   # 404

options.name: jetlink — URL shortener with click stats
options.detail: Shorten, redirect, count clicks, top-N stats endpoint. Same persistence/serde spread as A plus redirects; slightly thinner domain logic (fewer honest error paths than paste bodies + expiry).
options.code:
$ curl -d '{"url": "https://jet.dev/docs"}' localhost:8080/shorten
{"short": "http://localhost:8080/r/a7Kq"}
$ curl -i localhost:8080/r/a7Kq
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://jet.dev/docs

options.name: jetfeed — feed aggregator with background fetchers
options.detail: Background tasks poll RSS/JSON feeds via the HTTP client; the server serves a merged digest. Uniquely shows client+server+taskgroup in one program. Depends on outside networks for real runs, so its golden path needs local fixture feeds.
options.code:
$ jetfeed --feeds feeds.toml &
[fetch] lobste.rs ok (12 items)  [fetch] hn ok (30 items)
$ curl localhost:8080/digest | head -3
{"items": [{"title": "Jet 1.0 released", ...}

options.name: jetboard — kanban/task JSON API (pairs with the web slice)
options.detail: Boards/cards CRUD API. If the web slice is jettasks (D-FLAGSHIP3=A), this becomes its persistence backend — the two slices then demo a full-stack Jet story. Cost: the two pillars' fates couple; a change in one ripples into the other's goldens.

options.name: jetrelay — webhook receiver and fan-out
options.detail: Receives webhooks, verifies signatures (core.crypto), fans out to configured targets with retry. Ops-flavored and shows crypto + retry + concurrency; but its interesting behavior (retries, downstream failures) is the hardest to demo convincingly in a golden test.

decisions.comparisons: Go's proof was 'a static binary serving HTTP' (Docker, Caddy). Rust points at axum examples; TS at Express/Next starters. The convincing form is always a small, complete, deployable service — not a framework tour.
decisions.rec: A — CRUD + persistence + expiry covers the widest honest surface (db, serde, time, routes, logs, shutdown) while every proof stays curl-observable and golden-testable.
decisions.recommendation: A — CRUD + persistence + expiry covers the widest honest surface (db, serde, time, routes, logs, shutdown) while every proof stays curl-observable and golden-testable.

decisions.gist: Which browser app is Jet's flagship web slice — the WASM/reactive-UI program people compare against React/Svelte.
decisions.story: Betty writes React at work. She'll take Jet-on-the-web seriously the moment she can read one app she already knows by heart and see the Jet version is shorter, typed end-to-end, and has no npm folder. What app we pick decides whether that comparison is even possible.
decisions.detail: [Owner 2026-07-03: flagship slices deferred to END of Epoch 4 — jetpack development takes priority. Web-app slice candidate when resumed: recreate Tower itself in Jet (owner suggestion, recorded on card #9).]

options.name: jettasks — TodoMVC (recommended)
options.detail: The TodoMVC spec, exactly: add/toggle/edit/delete, filters, clear-completed, count footer, keyboard interaction, persisted to browser storage. Instantly comparable to every framework a web dev knows; exercises signals, view tree, typed styles, components, a11y lint, and browser storage.

$ jet dev app/main.jet --target=web
  serving http://localhost:8080  (live reload)

decisions.title: Style length spelling: unit literals vs Length wrappers vs bare numbers
decisions.gist: How a user writes a length like 320 pixels in a UI style.
decisions.story: Betty is laying out the settings page of her recipe app: a card 320 wide, 180 tall, 12 of padding. She wants to type those three numbers once, have the compiler catch a unit typo, and not wonder later whether 320 meant pixels or something else.

options.name: Unit-family literal: width: 320px (recommended)
options.detail: core.ui.style declares a #UnitFamily(length) { px } (D-QUAL3), so the ratified unit-literal syntax (D-UNITLIT1) applies: 320px is a compile-checked Px value. One canonical unit mechanism in the whole language (I8) — style lengths use the same machinery as 500ms and 12.50usd. Unit typos are compile errors (E0134); if a second unit ever ships, cross-unit math is a compile error too (E0127). Reads like the CSS every beginner has already seen.

options.name: Enum with per-unit variants: width: .Px.{value: 320.0}
options.detail: Length is an enum whose variants carry the value: Length { Px(value: Float) }. Fully typed and pattern-matchable, and the field type stays a single Length even if more units are added. But it duplicates what unit families already do with a second, style-only mechanism (I8), and every length costs a variant-construction spelling.

options.name: Flat pair record: width: Length.{value: 320.0, unit: .Px}
options.detail: Length is a two-field struct (value + LengthUnit enum) — the shape Phase 3's example shipped. Plain user-space types, nothing new to learn beyond structs. But it's the most ceremony per length, the unit and value can be read independently without matching (a backend can use .value and forget .unit), and it's a second unit mechanism next to unit families (I8).

options.name: Bare Float logical pixels: width: 320.0
options.detail: No Length type at all — style dimensions are Float, pixels by convention, like SwiftUI/Flutter. Least typing and no unit concept for beginners to learn. But the unit lives in documentation instead of the type: 320.0 could be anything, a duration mixed into a width compiles fine, and adding real units later changes every Style field's type.

options.name: CSS string: width: "320px"
options.detail: Lengths are strings parsed at render time, exactly like inline CSS. Familiar to web developers and trivially copy-pasteable from CSS. But every typo becomes a runtime failure in the user's running app, the compiler can't help with math on lengths, and stringly-typed values are the opposite of the typed-styles goal this phase exists for.

decisions.comparisons:
CSS:            width: 320px;              — unit-suffix literal, the shape every web tutorial teaches
Jetpack Compose: Modifier.width(320.dp)     — typed Dp via extension property; 320 alone is a type error
SwiftUI:        .frame(width: 320)         — unitless CGFloat points, unit is implicit convention
Flutter:        SizedBox(width: 320)       — unitless logical pixels, same implicit convention
React inline:   {{ width: 320 }}           — bare number silently means px; {{ width: '320px' }} string also accepted
Typst:          width: 320pt               — unit-suffix literal, checked at compile time
decisions.rec: A — reuses the one ratified unit mechanism (D-QUAL3 + D-UNITLIT1), so `320px` is compile-checked with zero ceremony and no second style-only unit system (I8).
decisions.recommendation: A — reuses the one ratified unit mechanism (D-QUAL3 + D-UNITLIT1), so `320px` is compile-checked with zero ceremony and no second style-only unit system (I8).

decisions.title: How does ungated code get "the impl for this OS"?
decisions.gist: #Target(Os.*) now gates impls, but plain main has no ratified way to construct/dispatch to whichever gated impl survived the build.
decisions.story: Doris writes a desktop app. She gates LinuxBackend and MacosBackend impls per D-OSTARGET1. Now her ungated main needs a backend value. Constructing LinuxBackend directly in main is (correctly) E-OSTARGET-UNMATCHED-CALL — main is not Linux-only. There is no blessed way to say "give me the one that matched this build."

options.name: fn-level #Target(Os.*) + one-survivor rule (recommended)
options.detail: Extend gating to fns: several fns share one name/signature, each gated to a different OS, exactly one survives per build; ungated code calls it like any fn. Missing an OS the build targets = compile error listing covered OSes. Mirrors Rust cfg/Go build tags; no new expression syntax.

options.name: Comptime OS switch expression
options.detail: A compiler-known comptime value (e.g. build.os) usable in a match whose non-matching arms are discarded before OS-gating checks run. More general (any per-OS choice), but new comptime surface + a second way to express what A does (I8 pressure).

options.name: Status quo — gated modules own the choice
options.detail: Ungated code never touches gated types; each app ships a per-OS gated module exporting a common fn. Works today only if fn-level gating exists somewhere, which it does not — effectively forces apps to gate their whole main, hollowing the check.
options.code: // every call chain from main must itself be OS-gated — main per OS.

comparisons.note: #[cfg(target_os)] fns — one survives per build.
build tags: one file per OS defines the same fn.
comparisons.code:
//go:build linux
func newBackend() Backend { return gtk{} }

comparisons.note: comptime switch on builtin.os.
comparisons.code: const b = switch (builtin.os.tag) { .linux => Gtk{}, .macos => AppKit{}, else => unreachable };

decisions.rec: A — smallest ratified-shape extension (same marker, fns instead of impls), proven pattern in Rust/Go, keeps one dispatch idiom (I8).
decisions.recommendation: A — smallest ratified-shape extension (same marker, fns instead of impls), proven pattern in Rust/Go, keeps one dispatch idiom (I8).

decisions.gist: How you ask the compiler to show the facts it proved (inline decisions, resolved ref owners) — the command's exact shape and what it does with no lens named.
decisions.story: Doris maintains a telemetry indexer. A teammate's PR adds `@InlineAlways` to a hot dot-product and a new `&Incident` field whose owner the compiler inferred. Before approving, Doris wants to SEE what the compiler decided — which calls actually inlined, which arena owns that field — without reading generated Rust. Three ratified decisions promised her `jet expand --facts`; this ballot fixes the command's final shape.

options.name: jet expand --facts <lens>; bare expand shows everything (recommended)
options.detail: Exactly the surface the three ratified decisions name. `--facts <lens>` narrows to one lens; bare `jet expand <file>` runs every lens, grouped — the magic default is 'show me all of it'. `--json` (existing global flag) emits the stable semindex-schema document. Unknown lens lists the valid ones.
options.code:
$ jet expand src/index.jet
inline — call-site decisions (2 facts)
  src/render.jet:41:15  Vec3.dot  inlined (@InlineAlways)
  src/hot.jet:88:9      Vec3.dot  inlined (@InlineAlways)

refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  src/index.jet:12:5  Index.hot      owner: pool       (labeled @Ref(pool))
  src/index.jet:13:5  Index.cold     owner: arena      (labeled @Ref(arena))

$ jet expand --facts refs src/index.jet
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  ...

$ jet expand --facts spam src/index.jet
error: no lens named `spam`
 Fix: pick one — inline (call-site inline decisions), refs (resolved ref/view owners)

options.name: jet expand --facts <lens>; bare expand is a lens directory, name reserved
options.detail: Same ratified `--facts <lens>` spelling, but bare `jet expand <file>` prints the lens menu and exits nonzero instead of dumping everything. Keeps the bare name free for Epoch-4 derive/macro expansion audit (D-METHODMACRO1 routed DSL power there), so `jet expand` can later mean 'show generated code' without a meaning change breaking scripts.
options.code:
$ jet expand src/index.jet
error: `jet expand` needs a lens
 What: available lenses —
   inline  call-site inline decisions
   refs    resolved ref/view owners
 Fix: jet expand --facts refs src/index.jet

$ jet expand --facts inline src/index.jet
inline — call-site decisions (2 facts)
  src/render.jet:41:15  Vec3.dot  inlined (@InlineAlways)
  src/hot.jet:88:9      Vec3.dot  inlined (@InlineAlways)

options.name: positional lens: jet expand <lens> <file>
options.detail: Drop the flag; the lens is the first word, like `jet schema status`. Reads faster and matches subcommand-verb muscle memory. REQUIRES AMENDING the transparency wording of D-METHODMACRO1, D-REF-SHORTHAND1, and D-DYNARRAY1, which all ratified the literal spelling `jet expand --facts <lens>`.
options.code:
$ jet expand refs src/index.jet
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  ...

$ jet expand src/index.jet        // lens word missing
error: `jet expand` needs a lens: inline | refs
 Fix: jet expand refs src/index.jet

options.name: dedicated subcommand: jet facts <lens> <file>
options.detail: The command is about facts, so name it that; `expand` stays unclaimed until Epoch-4 code expansion actually exists. Clean noun, discoverable in `jet help`. REQUIRES AMENDING the three ratified decisions' `jet expand --facts` wording.
options.code:
$ jet facts refs src/index.jet
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  ...

$ jet facts src/index.jet          // no lens: run them all
inline — call-site decisions (2 facts)
  ...
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  ...

options.name: fold into semindex: jet semindex <file> --facts <lens>
options.detail: The facts already live in the semantic index (D-SEMINDEX1); expose the lens there instead of minting a command. One tool for 'ask the index'. Costs beginners the discoverable verb — `semindex` is tooling vocabulary, not a word Doris would guess. REQUIRES AMENDING the three ratified decisions' wording.
options.code:
$ jet semindex src/index.jet --facts refs
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  ...

$ jet semindex src/index.jet       // unchanged: index summary
semantic index (schema v2)
  definitions: 14
  ...

options.name: check-mode flag: jet check <file> --facts <lens>
options.detail: Facts fall out of checking, so hang them on `jet check` — one compile, diagnostics plus facts in a single run, nothing new in `jet help`'s top level. Muddles check's contract (exit status = did it compile) with a reporting surface, and buries the transparency story the ballots sold as its own command. REQUIRES AMENDING the three ratified decisions' wording.
options.code:
$ jet check src/index.jet --facts refs
ok: src/index.jet checks clean

refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  ...

decisions.comparisons: Rust: `cargo expand` (nightly, macro output only) and `rustc --emit=mir` — dumps of transformed code, not curated facts; inlining is invisible. C: `gcc -E` preprocessed soup. Jai: metaprogram message loop can print build facts, but there's no standard lens command. Swift: `-emit-sil` expert dump. Nobody ships a beginner-readable 'what did the compiler decide' surface; Jet's is per-fact lines with file:line, plus `--json` for tools.
decisions.rec: A — the only shape that honors all three ratified decisions verbatim (no amendment churn), and bare `jet expand` showing every lens is the right magic default: the beginner who doesn't know lens names still gets the answer, the expert narrows with --facts.
decisions.recommendation: A — the only shape that honors all three ratified decisions verbatim (no amendment churn), and bare `jet expand` showing every lens is the right magic default: the beginner who doesn't know lens names still gets the answer, the expert narrows with --facts.

decisions.title: Should decode apply migration{} blocks to old stored data at runtime?
decisions.gist: Old stored data currently fails to decode; should the compiler generate the code that upgrades it in place during decode?
decisions.story: Betty (from D-MIGRATE3) ships schema v3 of UserRecord. Her nightly import reads three-year-old v1 JSON. Today that decode simply errors — the migration blocks she wrote only prove a migration EXISTS at compile time. She expected the old records to load and upgrade; decode_traced exists to tell her it happened, but nothing can happen yet.

options.name: Generate the migration chain into decode (recommended)
options.detail: Codegen lowers each migration{} block to a step function; decode of a @PublishedSchema type first tries the current shape, on mismatch walks stored version tags/shape detection oldest to current, applying steps. decode_traced records from+steps; plain decode applies silently. Zero cost for types without migrations (nothing generated).

options.name: Explicit opt-in call: decode_migrating only
options.detail: Plain decode keeps failing on old shapes; a third method decode_migrating<T> applies the chain. Callers must choose migration explicitly; surface grows to three decode verbs (I8 pressure).
options.code:
user :: json.decode_migrating<UserRecord>(raw)?   // applies chain
old  :: json.decode<UserRecord>(raw)               // still errors on v1

options.name: Defer past Epoch 3 (status quo)
options.detail: Keep compile-time-only checks; decode_traced stays always-false until a later epoch. Stored-data users must hand-write upgraders.
options.code:
// no change; v1 JSON keeps failing:
user :: json.decode<UserRecord>(raw) ?? panic("DecodeError")

comparisons.note: serde has no built-in versioning; versioning crates bolt it on manually.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct UserRecord { /* one shape only; old JSON = error */ }

comparisons.note: wire-level field ids + defaults make old data readable by construction.
comparisons.code: message UserRecord { int64 id = 1; string display_name = 2; bool verified = 3; }

comparisons.note: Codable: manual init(from:) branching on version keys.
comparisons.code: init(from d: Decoder) throws { /* if v1 { … } else { … } */ }

decisions.rec: A — the authoring surface (migration verbs) and the transparency surface (decode_traced) are both ratified and shipped; A is the semantics both were designed around, keeps one decode verb (I8), and costs nothing for unversioned types.
decisions.recommendation: A — the authoring surface (migration verbs) and the transparency surface (decode_traced) are both ratified and shipped; A is the semantics both were designed around, keeps one decode verb (I8), and costs nothing for unversioned types.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in tools/Tower/docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: I still have absolutely no clue what this means. Give me a user story with example code so I can learn what you mean
questions.answer: Ratified A (2026-06-20). Not a language feature — a naming clash inside our own spec docs. Two ratified decisions both coined "Layer 2": S26 (derive ladder: built-in derives) and S60 (capability tier: compile-time pure eval + data embedding). A keeps both numbers and adds one cross-reference sentence on S60 so the next reader can tell them apart. No code, no rename. Compile-time embedding work files under S60.

questions.text: I am leaning B but want to understand the practical tradeoofs of going with B & C respectively
questions.answer: Ratified B (2026-06-20). B (stdlib Guard value: scope.guard(() => {…})) delivers ~95% of C's value — cleanup on every exit path including the ? early return — for zero new syntax and zero ratification, running on existing Drop + lambda machinery, and keeps Jet's one-cleanup-story (RAII) intact. questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.
